extraction.body: It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics. “The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems. The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory. Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip . Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this … But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯. It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified. Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully. Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding. Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue. Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer. Meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.” Without being expressed in Lean, it is too early to say whether the proof checks out, much less if anyone understands it. In a brief introduction to his proof, which he said is the result of 12 years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.” This story has been updated to include that Alpöge’s Lean proof has been checked by independent sources. extraction.body: Two mathematicians have put forward competing claims involving one of mathematics' most famous unsolved problems, the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, setting up an unusual contest over whether artificial intelligence or human mathematical reasoning can crack a question that has challenged generations of researchers. Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at artificial intelligence company Anthropic, said he had discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis with the help of the company's AI model Claude. His announcement on November 20 was followed by a separate proposed proof of the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) by Alessandro Maria Masullo, a Stanford researcher, which was described by Stanford mathematician Ravi Vakil as entirely human-developed, without AI assistance. The two claims are at different stages of scrutiny. Alpöge's work has cleared several important computer-based verification checks, while Masullo's proposed proof has encountered questions from mathematicians examining the draft. Alpöge released a four-page note and a 14-part archive containing approximately 17.4 million lines of code written in Lean, a programming language used to formalise and verify mathematical proofs. He said the work also establishes the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions. The scale of the formalisation presents an unusual challenge: Alpöge said a conventional written version of the argument could run to more than 250,000 pages. There has, however, been progress in checking the claim. Andrew Sutherland, a mathematics professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, reported that all 175,187 modules in Alpöge's Lean archive compiled without errors. The proof also passed checks by independently developed verification systems, including nanoda and con-leche, as well as lean4lean. Some checks, including a full Comparator run and additional Lean-kernel verification, were still underway in Sutherland's November 20 update. The machine checks establish that the formalised statements follow from the specified mathematical definitions and standard axioms; mathematicians still need to understand and assess the argument. The competing human-developed claim emerged through Vakil, who said Masullo's proposed proof of GRH had been examined by Stanford mathematician Brian Conrad over several months. extraction.body: It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics. “The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems. The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory. Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip . Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this … But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯. It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified. Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully. Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding. Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue. Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer. Meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.” Without being expressed in Lean, it is too early to say whether the proof checks out, much less if anyone understands it. In a brief introduction to his proof, which he said is the result of 12 years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.” This story has been updated to include that Alpöge’s Lean proof has been checked by independent sources. extraction.body: Two mathematicians have put forward competing claims involving one of mathematics' most famous unsolved problems, the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, setting up an unusual contest over whether artificial intelligence or human mathematical reasoning can crack a question that has challenged generations of researchers. Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at artificial intelligence company Anthropic, said he had discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis with the help of the company's AI model Claude. His announcement on November 20 was followed by a separate proposed proof of the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) by Alessandro Maria Masullo, a Stanford researcher, which was described by Stanford mathematician Ravi Vakil as entirely human-developed, without AI assistance. The two claims are at different stages of scrutiny. Alpöge's work has cleared several important computer-based verification checks, while Masullo's proposed proof has encountered questions from mathematicians examining the draft. Alpöge released a four-page note and a 14-part archive containing approximately 17.4 million lines of code written in Lean, a programming language used to formalise and verify mathematical proofs. He said the work also establishes the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions. The scale of the formalisation presents an unusual challenge: Alpöge said a conventional written version of the argument could run to more than 250,000 pages. There has, however, been progress in checking the claim. Andrew Sutherland, a mathematics professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, reported that all 175,187 modules in Alpöge's Lean archive compiled without errors. The proof also passed checks by independently developed verification systems, including nanoda and con-leche, as well as lean4lean. Some checks, including a full Comparator run and additional Lean-kernel verification, were still underway in Sutherland's November 20 update. The machine checks establish that the formalised statements follow from the specified mathematical definitions and standard axioms; mathematicians still need to understand and assess the argument. The competing human-developed claim emerged through Vakil, who said Masullo's proposed proof of GRH had been examined by Stanford mathematician Brian Conrad over several months. However, in an update posted later on November 20, Vakil said several mathematicians had reported problems in the draft, identified with assistance from different AI models. He said the issues would need to be resolved before the proof could be accepted. First proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis is a mathematical theory about the pattern in which prime numbers appear. Prime numbers, such as 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11, are divisible only by themselves and 1. Although they appear randomly as numbers get larger, mathematicians believe there is an underlying pattern governing their distribution. Riemann's hypothesis attempts to explain that pattern through a mathematical function called the Riemann zeta function. In simple terms, it predicts that a particular set of solutions, known as the non-trivial zeros of this function, all fall on one specific line in a mathematical plane. Proving this would help mathematicians understand much more precisely how prime numbers are distributed. The problem is among seven major mathematical challenges identified by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000. Each carries a $1 million prize for a valid solution. However, a proposed proof must first be published in a qualifying peer-reviewed journal, undergo at least two years of scrutiny and gain broad acceptance among mathematicians before the prize can be awarded. The two claims are at different stages of scrutiny. Alpöge's work has cleared several important computer-based verification checks, while Masullo's proposed proof has encountered questions from mathematicians examining the draft.

The scale of the formalisation presents an unusual challenge: Alpöge said a conventional written version of the argument could run to more than 250,000 pages.

There has, however, been progress in checking the claim. Andrew Sutherland, a mathematics professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, reported that all 175,187 modules in Alpöge's Lean archive compiled without errors. The proof also passed checks by independently developed verification systems, including nanoda and con-leche, as well as lean4lean.

Some checks, including a full Comparator run and additional Lean-kernel verification, were still underway in Sutherland's November 20 update. The machine checks establish that the formalised statements follow from the specified mathematical definitions and standard axioms; mathematicians still need to understand and assess the argument.

The competing human-developed claim emerged through Vakil, who said Masullo's proposed proof of GRH had been examined by Stanford mathematician Brian Conrad over several months. However, in an update posted later on November 20, Vakil said several mathematicians had reported problems in the draft, identified with assistance from different AI models. He said the issues would need to be resolved before the proof could be accepted.

First proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis is a mathematical theory about the pattern in which prime numbers appear. Prime numbers, such as 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11, are divisible only by themselves and 1. Although they appear randomly as numbers get larger, mathematicians believe there is an underlying pattern governing their distribution. Riemann's hypothesis attempts to explain that pattern through a mathematical function called the Riemann zeta function.

In simple terms, it predicts that a particular set of solutions, known as the non-trivial zeros of this function, all fall on one specific line in a mathematical plane. Proving this would help mathematicians understand much more precisely how prime numbers are distributed.

The problem is among seven major mathematical challenges identified by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000. Each carries a $1 million prize for a valid solution. However, a proposed proof must first be published in a qualifying peer-reviewed journal, undergo at least two years of scrutiny and gain broad acceptance among mathematicians before the prize can be awarded.

It'll also be a contender for the Millennium Prize, which offers a $1 million prize for solving seven major math problems (including the Riemann Hypothesis).

"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line.
No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line," he says.
Referring to Anthropic's recent IPO, Alpöge also says the "timing is horrible" — because it could lead some to conclude that the findings are somewhat contrived.
"This problem has been the sacred object in mathematics for me since my childhood, and I am very touchy about the treatment of great intellectual goals," he added.

The proposed proof also addresses the generalised Riemann hypothesis, a broader version of the original conjecture.The claim has drawn attention from leading mathematicians, although the proof still needs wider independent scrutiny and a deeper understanding of its mathematical reasoning. James Maynard, the Regius Professor of Mathematics at the University of Oxford and a 2022 Fields Medal winner, expressed optimism about the result.“If this fully checks out, it is clearly a historic milestone in mathematics, establishing one of the great mysteries of the subject,” Maynard told IBM Think in an interview. “This result really stands out, even in the context of all the recent AI breakthroughs.”Alpöge shared the proposed proof in Lean, a programming language and proof assistant that checks mathematical arguments step by step. The format allows researchers to examine whether each part of the reasoning follows logically, although verifying the computer-checked argument and understanding the ideas behind it are separate challenges.In a statement posted on his website, Alpöge wrote: “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.”What is the Riemann hypothesis?First proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers, which are divisible only by themselves and one. Examples include 2, 3 and 5.Although prime numbers appear to occur irregularly along the number line, the Riemann hypothesis predicts that their distribution follows a deeper mathematical pattern. Each carries a prize of $1 million for a correct solution.Alpöge's announcement follows a series of AI-assisted advances in mathematics, with large language models increasingly being used to explore complex conjectures and theoretical problems. The latest claim, if verified, would represent a major step beyond earlier results that established the predicted pattern for only a proportion of certain mathematical values.Why the proposed proof mattersYouness Lamzouri, a professor of mathematics at the University of Lorraine in France, said the proposed result would go substantially further than an earlier AI-assisted breakthrough.Previous work had established that at least 67.25% of a particular set of mathematical values followed the pattern predicted by the Riemann hypothesis. The new claim, if correct, would establish that all of them follow the pattern without exception.Lamzouri, who developed a shorter proof of the earlier result without AI, said the latest announcement had left him astonished.“I don’t have words to describe what I am feeling right now. “If this claim happens to be true, it will be a huge achievement.”However, he cautioned that checking the computer-generated proof would only be the first step. Mathematicians would also need to understand the reasoning and ideas behind it before accepting its broader implications.“Mathematics is mainly about understanding why something is true,” he said. I know there will be a wide range of reactions in our community, but to me this is a human triumph, and a day for celebration.”Sutherland said the achievement should also be viewed in the context of the human work behind the development of Lean, large language models and centuries of mathematical research.“There is much work to be done to understand the mathematical details of the proof,” he said. But perhaps the single most important step in the proof was building a machine that can think.”A turning point for AI-assisted mathematics?Alpöge's claim comes after a year of growing attention on the ability of AI models to tackle difficult mathematical problems. He had earlier attracted attention in July after sharing a Claude-generated solution to the Jacobian conjecture. He was also involved in a September controversy surrounding an OpenAI mathematical result related to the Navier-Stokes problem.If the Riemann hypothesis proof is independently verified and its reasoning understood, it could mark a major advance in the use of AI for mathematical discovery. The result would not necessarily have immediate practical applications, but it could reshape research in number theory and deepen understanding of connections across mathematics.For now, the central question is whether the proposed proof withstands independent examination. Even if the computer verification holds, mathematicians will need to establish why the argument works and what new avenues it opens.You use AI every day.

extraction.body: Hyderabad: An Anthropic mathematician says he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of the hardest problems in mathematics, with the help of the company s Artificial Intelligence (AI) model, Claude. If the proof is confirmed, it would be another major moment for AI in mathematics.Levent Alpoge made the claim on his own website. His work has not yet been checked by independent experts, and Anthropic has not commented on it or taken part in his announcement. What Alpoge says?In a note on his website, Alpoge said he believes he and Claude found a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. He added that the method could go further, solving a wider version called the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis. He also expects it to solve the Extended Riemann Hypothesis given more time.He said he and Claude have also formalised the arguments in Lean, a computer language used to write mathematical proofs. Alpoge says he texted Anthropic s chief executive officer (CEO) Dario Amodei about the solution late on Sunday night. He also suggests he waited until the company s share launch on Thursday before publishing. Also Read: Anthropic Surges In Market Debut After Biggest IPO On Record, Despite Fears That AI Is Running AmokWhy the problem matters?The Riemann hypothesis was first put forward in 1859. It deals with how prime numbers are spread out and how the zeros of a certain function are linked to them. Many experts see it as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.It is also one of seven Millennium Prize problems. The Clay Mathematics Institute offers a $1 million prize for each one that is solved.A long road to recognitionEven if the proof is right, a prize is a long way off. Under the institute s rules, a solution must be published and survive at least two years of close study. It was the Poincaré conjecture, which is about three-dimensional spheres.Anthropic s earlier viewAnthropic has said in August that it was working on the Riemann hypothesis with Claude. At the time, the company said it did not expect the methods Claude used to lead to a proof.Also Read: From Wearable Agent To Heavy Coding: Top AI Releases From Meta, Google, OpenAI, And AnthropicThe wider AI race in mathematicsIt is worth noting that the Riemann hypothesis proof comes as AI firms push deeper into mathematics. OpenAI said it went after that problem after hearing that rival researchers were close to a solution. Alpoge had been working on it with Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematics professor at New York University. Buckmaster said OpenAI reached its answer using the same route the two men had been following with OpenAI s Codex and Claude.OpenAI reportedly spent millions of dollars and used 10,000 AI agents on the task. Many people see its result as credible, though it has not yet been formally recognised.The work has also been hit by serious claims. Some say OpenAI used unpublished research from mathematicians who had shared it with its AI tools. OpenAI strongly denies any wrongdoing, but the row has not died down.Alpoge also said in July that he had solved the Jacobian conjecture using Claude. With so many claims arriving so quickly, mathematicians are struggling to keep up. They are also trying to work out where they fit in a field that is changing fast.For now, Alpoge s proof is only a claim. Experts will need time to test it, and its fate will show whether AI can truly crack problems that have stumped people for more than a century and a half.Also Read: Anthropic Expands Claude Into Spreadsheets, Dashboards, And Collaborative Workplace Tools

coreStoryFacts.text: In the same week that Anthropic was floated on the Nasdaq in its initial public offering , a mathematician employed by the company claims to have discovered proof behind one of the world's most famous math problem, the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis.
"An astounding amount of mathematics is present in the argument, far more than I had imagined would be necessary as a student," he writes.
Proposed in 1859 by Bernhard Riemann, who gave the problem its name, it is the theory that prime numbers are not in fact random but determined.
Alpöge's statement is not without reservation.
Aside from confirming whether Claude has actually helped crack the Riemann Hypothesis, which will take some time, he admits sadness at the finding.

"It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater."

When he's not at work, he loves reading about history and playing video games.
Earlier this year, OpenAI helped create a breakthrough solution for the Navier-Stokes problem, a finding somewhat overshadowed by a plagiarism controversy .
Anthropic has been busy celebrating the incredible numbers from its record-breaking $1.7tn stock market debut on Thursday.
But one of its mathematicians has been setting records of a very different kind — they claim to have used Claude AI to prove a 167-year-old mathematics theory that's stumped professors for decades.
One thing's for sure — 2027 is going to be a very interesting year indeed for math and the sciences.
This is likely the start of a new math journey, where the proof will need to be vetted independently by other mathematicians and experts in the field.
It'll also be a contender for the Millennium Prize, which offers a $1 million prize for solving seven major math problems (including the Riemann Hypothesis).
However, the competition's rules state that proofs need "two years of scrutiny" before a potential payout.
The discovery is a sign of what can be achieved when the world's best researchers are given access to the world's best frontier models.
This theory is based on the conundrum of prime numbers and proposes that there might be a hidden pattern behind them.
In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too.
"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line.
No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line," he says.
Referring to Anthropic's recent IPO, Alpöge also says the "timing is horrible" — because it could lead some to conclude that the findings are somewhat contrived.
"This problem has been the sacred object in mathematics for me since my childhood, and I am very touchy about the treatment of great intellectual goals," he added.

passages: Anthropic has been busy celebrating the incredible numbers from its record-breaking $1.7tn stock market debut on Thursday.
But one of its mathematicians has been setting records of a very different kind — they claim to have used Claude AI to prove a 167-year-old mathematics theory that's stumped professors for decades.
One thing's for sure — 2027 is going to be a very interesting year indeed for math and the sciences.
This is likely the start of a new math journey, where the proof will need to be vetted independently by other mathematicians and experts in the field.
It'll also be a contender for the Millennium Prize, which offers a $1 million prize for solving seven major math problems (including the Riemann Hypothesis).
However, the competition's rules state that proofs need "two years of scrutiny" before a potential payout.
The discovery is a sign of what can be achieved when the world's best researchers are given access to the world's best frontier models.
This theory is based on the conundrum of prime numbers and proposes that there might be a hidden pattern behind them.
In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too.
"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line.
No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line," he says.
Referring to Anthropic's recent IPO, Alpöge also says the "timing is horrible" — because it could lead some to conclude that the findings are somewhat contrived.
"This problem has been the sacred object in mathematics for me since my childhood, and I am very touchy about the treatment of great intellectual goals," he added.

Anthropic has been busy celebrating the incredible numbers from its record-breaking $1.7tn stock market debut on Thursday. But one of its mathematicians has been setting records of a very different kind — they claim to have used Claude AI to prove a 167-year-old mathematics theory that's stumped professors for decades.

Levent Alpöge, an eminent Anthropic researcher who specializes in number theory, published a statement on his personal website today that claims to have solved the 'Riemann hypothesis'. This theory is based on the conundrum of prime numbers and proposes that there might be a hidden pattern behind them.

In his statement, the Harvard-educated mathematician says: "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too.

"It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater," he added. Just another quiet day at the office, then.

There isn't currently a human-readable version of Alpöge's proof of the hypothesis, only a version in Lean (the open-source programming language). That's partly because "an astounding amount of mathematics is present in the argument", according to Alpöge, and he wanted to avoid publishing a "massive unreadable travesty of slop". An early draft apparently went over 250,000 pages.

This is likely the start of a new math journey, where the proof will need to be vetted independently by other mathematicians and experts in the field. It'll also be a contender for the Millennium Prize, which offers a $1 million prize for solving seven major math problems (including the Riemann Hypothesis). However, the competition's rules state that proofs need "two years of scrutiny" before a potential payout.
For now, it's potentially one of the most significant milestones yet in the so-called 'mathocalypse'.

It's hard to say which field AI is disrupting more right now — the worlds of IT and cybersecurity, which are dealing with record numbers of major outages that have been linked to the AI's talent for discovering vulnerabilities, or mathematics. But today's news is certainly more momentous than another Microsoft Outlook outage.

The discovery is a sign of what can be achieved when the world's best researchers are given access to the world's best frontier models. But Levent Alpöge modestly says that it was Claude that sparked the final breakthrough in his battle with this 167-year-old math problem.

"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line," he says. Referring to Anthropic's recent IPO, Alpöge also says the "timing is horrible" — because it could lead some to conclude that the findings are somewhat contrived.

"This problem has been the sacred object in mathematics for me since my childhood, and I am very touchy about the treatment of great intellectual goals," he added. "There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false, and I am pleased that I am in circumstances where it is obviously false," he concluded.

The announcement will no doubt leave mathematicians pondering what 2027 brings for their field. “Math has changed more in the last two months than in the last 100 years,” Bryna Kra, the Sarah Rebecca Roland Professor of Mathematics at Northwestern University, recent told the MIT. "It’s a really exciting moment … and also scary," he added.

For now, this apparent 'Riemann hypothesis' breakthrough will sit alongside moments like Anthropic's proof for Fermat's Last Theorem (first proposed back in 1637), Google Gemini's shattering of a 59-year-old nuclear fusion conjecture , and OpenAI publishing its proposal for the Navier-Stokes equation as part of a blitz of papers that some academics called a "giant bomb" . One thing's for sure — 2027 is going to be a very interesting year indeed for math and the sciences.

extraction.body: An Anthropic mathematician has claimed to have developed a proof of the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis with the help of the company's artificial intelligence model Claude, potentially marking a landmark moment for AI-assisted mathematical research.Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, announced on Friday that he believed he had solved the famous mathematical problem, which concerns the distribution of prime numbers and has remained unresolved since 1859. The proposed proof also addresses the generalised Riemann hypothesis, a broader version of the original conjecture.The claim has drawn attention from leading mathematicians, although the proof still needs wider independent scrutiny and a deeper understanding of its mathematical reasoning. James Maynard, the Regius Professor of Mathematics at the University of Oxford and a 2022 Fields Medal winner, expressed optimism about the result.“If this fully checks out, it is clearly a historic milestone in mathematics, establishing one of the great mysteries of the subject,” Maynard told IBM Think in an interview. “This result really stands out, even in the context of all the recent AI breakthroughs.”Alpöge shared the proposed proof in Lean, a programming language and proof assistant that checks mathematical arguments step by step. The format allows researchers to examine whether each part of the reasoning follows logically, although verifying the computer-checked argument and understanding the ideas behind it are separate challenges.In a statement posted on his website, Alpöge wrote: “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.”What is the Riemann hypothesis?First proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers, which are divisible only by themselves and one. Examples include 2, 3 and 5.Although prime numbers appear to occur irregularly along the number line, the Riemann hypothesis predicts that their distribution follows a deeper mathematical pattern. Each carries a prize of $1 million for a correct solution.Alpöge's announcement follows a series of AI-assisted advances in mathematics, with large language models increasingly being used to explore complex conjectures and theoretical problems. The latest claim, if verified, would represent a major step beyond earlier results that established the predicted pattern for only a proportion of certain mathematical values.Why the proposed proof mattersYouness Lamzouri, a professor of mathematics at the University of Lorraine in France, said the proposed result would go substantially further than an earlier AI-assisted breakthrough.Previous work had established that at least 67.25% of a particular set of mathematical values followed the pattern predicted by the Riemann hypothesis. The new claim, if correct, would establish that all of them follow the pattern without exception.Lamzouri, who developed a shorter proof of the earlier result without AI, said the latest announcement had left him astonished.“I don’t have words to describe what I am feeling right now. “If this claim happens to be true, it will be a huge achievement.”However, he cautioned that checking the computer-generated proof would only be the first step. Mathematicians would also need to understand the reasoning and ideas behind it before accepting its broader implications.“Mathematics is mainly about understanding why something is true,” he said. I know there will be a wide range of reactions in our community, but to me this is a human triumph, and a day for celebration.”Sutherland said the achievement should also be viewed in the context of the human work behind the development of Lean, large language models and centuries of mathematical research.“There is much work to be done to understand the mathematical details of the proof,” he said. But perhaps the single most important step in the proof was building a machine that can think.”A turning point for AI-assisted mathematics?Alpöge's claim comes after a year of growing attention on the ability of AI models to tackle difficult mathematical problems. He had earlier attracted attention in July after sharing a Claude-generated solution to the Jacobian conjecture. He was also involved in a September controversy surrounding an OpenAI mathematical result related to the Navier-Stokes problem.If the Riemann hypothesis proof is independently verified and its reasoning understood, it could mark a major advance in the use of AI for mathematical discovery. The result would not necessarily have immediate practical applications, but it could reshape research in number theory and deepen understanding of connections across mathematics.For now, the central question is whether the proposed proof withstands independent examination. Even if the computer verification holds, mathematicians will need to establish why the argument works and what new avenues it opens.You use AI every day.

passages: President Donald Trump addressed the reports during an interview Saturday with Fox News, saying, “We just heard about it and I will say that it’s not good.” At the same time, Trump also said that as a result of the breach, “maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise because, you know, you had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax.”

A former FBI official told CNN that they’re not just concerned about “whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an issue, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on.”
In September, the FBI reportedly told agents and support staff that their personal information had been stolen in a cyberattack .

extraction.body: WASHINGTON — The FBI is investigating an apparent cyberattack against its National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a critical law enforcement database, according to news reports Saturday, November 21, 2026. CNN first reported the intrusion, citing people familiar with the investigation. The Associated Press subsequently confirmed the investigation through another source. The FBI declined comment. The hackers’ identities, methods and whether sensitive information was stolen remain unknown. President Donald Trump addressed the incident during a Fox News interview. “We just heard about it and I will say that it’s not good,” Trump said. However, Trump suggested the breach might expose previously undisclosed information concerning investigations involving Russia, Ukraine and alleged election fraud. The NCIC is a nationwide computerized information-sharing network operated by the FBI. Federal, state and local police use it to identify fugitives, locate missing persons, check arrest warrants, examine criminal histories and identify stolen vehicles, firearms and other property. In November 2025, former Maryland sheriff’s deputy Dontae Odom received a six-month jail sentence for unauthorized searches involving romantic partners and others. In January 2025, former Bryant, Arkansas, officer Christopher Bennett was arrested for illegally accessing the state crime database. sources.title: FBI's national crime database targeted in hack, Trump says - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
passages: President Donald Trump said in an interview Saturday that the FBI’s National Crime Information Center database was targeted in a hack.

"Whether you’re a deputy sheriff in rural Tennessee, a state trooper working the interstate or an FBI agent investigating a fugitive, NCIC is how you check wanted persons, stolen vehicles, missing persons and other critical information," Pack told ABC News.
"Russia, if you're listening, I hope you're able to find the 30,000 emails that are missing," he said.
Russian hackers allegedly hacked Democratic National Committee emails during the summer of the 2016 campaign.
Then presidential candidate Trump said at the time he hoped Russian hackers reportedly responsible would also find thousands of private emails deleted by former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.
Trump made the claim during a phone interview with Fox News.
Pack said that he believed the FBI will have its best cyber investigators on the case.
"Officers need to know that when they run somebody through NCIC, the information coming back is accurate," he said.
"Because sometimes that information can mean the difference between an officer going home at the end of a shift or not."

extraction.body: President Donald Trump said in an interview Saturday that the FBI’s National Crime Information Center database was targeted in a hack. Trump made the claim during a phone interview with Fox News. "Well, we just heard about it, and I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he said during the interview. A law enforcement source confirmed to ABC News that the database was hacked. The NCIC is a repository of criminal justice information, including data on criminal record history, current fugitives, stolen property, and missing persons, according to the FBI. The perpetrators behind the hack and the scale of the intrusion are currently unclear. Federal, state, and local law enforcement use the database for their investigations, according to retired FBI Supervisory Special Agent Jason Pack. "Whether you’re a deputy sheriff in rural Tennessee, a state trooper working the interstate or an FBI agent investigating a fugitive, NCIC is how you check wanted persons, stolen vehicles, missing persons and other critical information," Pack told ABC News. "The FBI maintains the system, but it’s connected to law enforcement agencies all across the country. And that’s important when we start talking about how somebody might have gotten in," he added. Pack said that he believed the FBI will have its best cyber investigators on the case. "Officers need to know that when they run somebody through NCIC, the information coming back is accurate," he said. "Because sometimes that information can mean the difference between an officer going home at the end of a shift or not." During the interview, the president implied without providing evidence that the hack might include information related to the investigations into Russian interference into the 2016 election, which he has repeatedly called a "hoax," and the phone call he made to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy that led to his first impeachment by Congress. The NCIC would not have information regarding those investigations in its database. Russian hackers allegedly hacked Democratic National Committee emails during the summer of the 2016 campaign. Then presidential candidate Trump said at the time he hoped Russian hackers reportedly responsible would also find thousands of private emails deleted by former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. "Russia, if you're listening, I hope you're able to find the 30,000 emails that are missing," he said. Later, Trump said he was being sarcastic. sources.title: "Maybe we'll learn about the voter fraud": Trump puts his "positive spin" on FBI's National Crime Information Center hack - AOL.com
passages: President Donald Trump said on November 21, 2026, that the reported breach of the FBI’s National Crime Information Center (NCIC) was “not good,” then suggested that the hack could end up working in his favor.
He spoke by phone to Fox News’ Saturday in America , where host Kayleigh McEnany, his former White House press secretary, asked about the intrusion.
Thus, the voter fraud claim from President Trump came with no evidence attached, as it has before.
Multiple investigations have failed to substantiate widespread voter fraud, and officials in his own administration rejected those claims.
“But maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise.”
Trump said he had been briefed shortly before the call.
On the call with Kayleigh McEnany, Trump then turned to investigations he has attacked for years, framing the breach as a route to material he says the public has never seen.
CNN reported the FBI investigation on Friday night, citing two people briefed on the matter.
The NCIC is the system federal, state and local agencies use to share warrants and background check information.
It is the second breach of an FBI system in recent months.

Trump made the claim during a phone interview with Fox News. "Well, we just heard about it, and I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he said during the interview. A law enforcement source confirmed to ABC News that the database was hacked. The NCIC is a repository of criminal justice information, including data on criminal record history, current fugitives, stolen property, and missing persons, according to the FBI. The perpetrators behind the hack and the scale of the intrusion are currently unclear. Federal, state, and local law enforcement use the database for their investigations, according to retired FBI Supervisory Special Agent Jason Pack. "Whether you’re a deputy sheriff in rural Tennessee, a state trooper working the interstate or an FBI agent investigating a fugitive, NCIC is how you check wanted persons, stolen vehicles, missing persons and other critical information," Pack told ABC News. "The FBI maintains the system, but it’s connected to law enforcement agencies all across the country. And that’s important when we start talking about how somebody might have gotten in," he added. Pack said that he believed the FBI will have its best cyber investigators on the case. "Officers need to know that when they run somebody through NCIC, the information coming back is accurate," he said. "Because sometimes that information can mean the difference between an officer going home at the end of a shift or not." The NCIC would not have information regarding those investigations in its database. Russian hackers allegedly hacked Democratic National Committee emails during the summer of the 2016 campaign. extraction.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has downplayed U.S. fears that his firm's chips will aid the Chinese military, days ahead of another trip to the country as he attempts to walk a tightrope between Washington and Beijing. In an interview with CNN aired Sunday, Huang said "we don't have to worry about" China's military using U.S.-made technology because "they simply can't rely on it." "It could be limited at any time; not to mention, there's plenty of computing capacity in China already," Huang said. "They don't need Nvidia's chips, certainly, or American tech stacks in order to build their military," he said. The comments were made in reference to years of bipartisan U.S. policy that placed restrictions on semiconductor companies, prohibiting them from selling their most advanced artificial intelligence chips to clients in China. Huang also repeated past criticisms of the policies, arguing that the tactic of export controls has been counterproductive to the ultimate goal of U.S. tech leadership. "We want the American tech stack to be the global standard ... in order for us to do that, we have to be in search of all the AI developers in the world," Huang said, adding that half of the world's AI developers are in China. That means for America to be an AI leader, U.S. technology has to be available to all markets, including China, he added. Washington's latest restrictions on Nvidia's sales to China were implemented in April and are expected to result in billions in losses for the company. In May, Huang said chip restrictions had already cut Nvidia's China market share nearly in half . Huang's CNN interview came just days before he travels to China for his second trip to the country this year, and as Nvidia is reportedly working on another chip that is compliant with the latest export controls . Last week, the Nvidia CEO met with U.S. President Donald Trump , and was warned by U.S. lawmakers not to meet with companies connected to China's military or intelligence bodies, or entities named on America's restricted export list. According to Daniel Newman, CEO of tech advisory firm The Futurum Group, Huang's CNN interview exemplifies how Huang has been threading a needle between Washington and Beijing as it tries to maintain maximum market access. "He needs to walk a proverbial tightrope to make sure that he doesn't rattle the Trump administration," Newman said, adding that he also wants to be in a position for China to invest in Nvidia technology if and when the policy provides a better climate to do so. But that's not to say that his downplaying of Washington's concerns is valid, according to Newman. "I think it's hard to completely accept the idea that China couldn't use Nvidia's most advanced technologies for military use." He added that he would expect Nvidia's technology to be at the core of any country's AI training, including for use in the development of advanced weaponry. A U.S. official told Reuters last month that China's large language model startup DeepSeek — which says it used Nvidia chips to train its models — was supporting China's military and intelligence operations. On Sunday, Huang acknowledged there were concerns about DeepSeek's open-source R1 reasoning model being trained in China but said that there was no evidence that it presents dangers for that reason alone. Huang complimented the R1 reasoning model, calling it "revolutionary," and said its open-source nature has empowered startup companies, new industries and countries to be able to engage in AI. "The fact of the matter is, [China and the U.S.] are competitors, but we are highly interdependent, and to the extent that we can compete and both aspire to win, it is fine to respect our competitors," he concluded. extraction.body: Nvidia, Export Controls, China, AI Hardware, AI Policy CNN reviewed about 300 procurement notices: at least six US-blacklisted Chinese universities reported buying restricted Nvidia chips. What is confirmed and what is not. Short answer: A CNN review of business records found that at least six Chinese universities on the US Entity List have reported buying restricted Nvidia chips in recent years, including two military-linked schools that reported purchases in the last few months, according to CNN's report of November 19, 2026 . The amounts are small and mostly older chips, bought from obscure Chinese sellers. CNN could not verify delivery, and it is unclear how the sellers got the chips. The finding widens a story we covered earlier this month. Reuters reported on November 11 that one blacklisted school, Northwestern Polytechnical University, bought H200 chips (see our Northwestern Polytechnical coverage ). CNN says the number of universities involved and the full scope of purchases have not been reported before. CNN highlights the cases experts called most notable: "Those are the universities that have tight linkages to the Chinese military," Gregory Allen of Decision Tree Research told CNN, adding that military AI investment would start at such schools. Export-chip control gate behind which a chip rests, representing restricted Nvidia chips reaching blacklisted universities Under Chinese rules, public bodies must publish notices when they make certain purchases. CNN used a commercial database that collects them. It examined nearly 300 records from about 90 buyers: nearly 80% universities, nearly 14% research institutes, and some government agencies. CNN excluded purchases of computing power from overseas data centres, a loophole the Trump administration moved this week to close with new regulations. The limits are significant, and CNN states them. The records are likely incomplete because many institutions only publish notices locally or take them down quickly. The database does not hold every notice. And CNN could not verify that the hardware was delivered in each case. The notices give scant detail on the supply chain or on how the chips would be used. The report does not claim smuggling. It says it is unclear how the sellers acquired the chips. Kate Koren, a former US export control official now at CSIS, offered a possibility: some A100 chips may come "from stockpiles there before the controls were in place," because for a time they were not controlled under US law. A100 sales to China are banned now, but they were widely sold before 2022. She also describes how smuggling networks can work: "very sophisticated shell companies" with multiple hops, currency changes and falsified documents. That is a general description, not a finding about these universities. For a claimed-versus-verified look at one smuggling allegation involving Nvidia executives, see our Muddy Waters GPU diversion explainer . Under a policy set last year after lobbying by Nvidia, the US allows the H200 to be sold to entities in China case by case, with strict requirements to report the end user, per CNN. Experts quoted say officials are highly unlikely to approve sales to a blacklisted university. The Entity List bars shipments of controlled items without federal approval (the license requirements sit in 15 CFR Part 744 of the Export Administration Regulations ), and US rules oblige Nvidia and other suppliers to determine the end user and avoid chips reaching China. So a university on the list buying an H200 through a local reseller does not match an approved sale. It does not tell us whether Nvidia or an authorised distributor did anything wrong. The report does not accuse Nvidia of selling to these buyers. Three points stand out for people who follow AI hardware. Because the whole story rests on these notices, it helps to know what they are. A Chinese public university that buys equipment above a set value must publish a notice, usually on its own procurement page or a government platform. The notice typically names the buyer, the item, the quantity, the price in yuan and the winning supplier. It rarely says where the supplier got the item, who will use it, or whether delivery happened. That is why the same record can support two stories. A cautious reading says a school ordered a chip and a reseller won the order. A stronger reading says restricted hardware reached a military-linked campus. The first is what the notice shows; the second needs proof of delivery and of the chip's path, which CNN did not have. Prices give a small clue: roughly $60,000 per H200 in the Northwestern Polytechnical notices, as CNN's totals imply, is the type of figure that suggests grey-market resale rather than a direct Nvidia sale, but that is our arithmetic on CNN's numbers, not a finding. Each step added buyers, not proof of a pipeline. The common thread is that the controls leave room at the retail edge of China's market, while large, cutting-edge shipments, which are the main worry, are harder to hide. Does this change what builders can buy? No. These are purchases inside China by blacklisted schools. Cloud and chip availability for ordinary buyers is not affected by this report. Will Nvidia be penalised? Nothing in the CNN report says so. Rules put the end-user check on suppliers, and enforcement is a Commerce Department matter. No action has been announced. Why do old chips matter? A100 and A800 are older, but they still train and run useful models. For a university lab that is enough to do real work, which is why the Entity List covers them. If you resell or procure accelerators, the practical lessons are plain. Check buyers against the Entity List before any sale. Keep an end-user record for each shipment. Be careful with intermediaries whose own supply trail you cannot see. A chip's journey can become a compliance question years later, as these notices show. We read CNN's full report (published November 19, 2026) and compared it with our earlier coverage of Reuters' November 11 report on Northwestern Polytechnical. We will update this post if the US government or Nvidia responds. Details are accurate as of November 19, 2026. Procurement records can change or be removed. On November 20, 2026 Republican Senator Tom Cotton told the Wall Street Journal that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick repeatedly ignored warnings that U.S. AI chips were being smuggled to China before the Nvidia scandal broke. Cotton declined to back Lutnick but stopped short of calling for his firing. This post cites Cotton's October 2025 letter and ties the quote to export-control stakes for GPU buyers. President Trump told reporters on November 20, 2026 that the United States wants only older chips sold to China and is discussing a comprehensive deal with Beijing. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC the same day that H200 sales policy continues as planned and Jensen Huang was not discussed in latest China talks. This post separates presidential remarks from Bessent's threshold line. On November 19, 2026 the House Foreign Affairs Committee used its Export Control Reform Act authority to publish Nvidia and AMD export license data for China. It says buyers requested 3.4 million AI chips as of May and Commerce approved more than 879,000. Here is what the committee said, what is still unclear and why it matters.

"Those are the universities that have tight linkages to the Chinese military," Gregory Allen of Decision Tree Research told CNN, adding that military AI investment would start at such schools.
Export-chip control gate behind which a chip rests, representing restricted Nvidia chips reaching blacklisted universities

Under Chinese rules, public bodies must publish notices when they make certain purchases. CNN used a commercial database that collects them. It examined nearly 300 records from about 90 buyers: nearly 80% universities, nearly 14% research institutes, and some government agencies. CNN excluded purchases of computing power from overseas data centres, a loophole the Trump administration moved this week to close with new regulations.

The limits are significant, and CNN states them. The records are likely incomplete because many institutions only publish notices locally or take them down quickly. The database does not hold every notice. And CNN could not verify that the hardware was delivered in each case. The notices give scant detail on the supply chain or on how the chips would be used.

The report does not claim smuggling. It says it is unclear how the sellers acquired the chips. Kate Koren, a former US export control official now at CSIS, offered a possibility: some A100 chips may come "from stockpiles there before the controls were in place," because for a time they were not controlled under US law. A100 sales to China are banned now, but they were widely sold before 2022.

She also describes how smuggling networks can work: "very sophisticated shell companies" with multiple hops, currency changes and falsified documents. That is a general description, not a finding about these universities. For a claimed-versus-verified look at one smuggling allegation involving Nvidia executives, see our Muddy Waters GPU diversion explainer .

Under a policy set last year after lobbying by Nvidia, the US allows the H200 to be sold to entities in China case by case, with strict requirements to report the end user, per CNN. Experts quoted say officials are highly unlikely to approve sales to a blacklisted university. The Entity List bars shipments of controlled items without federal approval (the license requirements sit in 15 CFR Part 744 of the Export Administration Regulations ), and US rules oblige Nvidia and other suppliers to determine the end user and avoid chips reaching China.

So a university on the list buying an H200 through a local reseller does not match an approved sale. It does not tell us whether Nvidia or an authorised distributor did anything wrong. The report does not accuse Nvidia of selling to these buyers.
Three points stand out for people who follow AI hardware.

Because the whole story rests on these notices, it helps to know what they are. A Chinese public university that buys equipment above a set value must publish a notice, usually on its own procurement page or a government platform. The notice typically names the buyer, the item, the quantity, the price in yuan and the winning supplier. It rarely says where the supplier got the item, who will use it, or whether delivery happened.

That is why the same record can support two stories. A cautious reading says a school ordered a chip and a reseller won the order. A stronger reading says restricted hardware reached a military-linked campus. The first is what the notice shows; the second needs proof of delivery and of the chip's path, which CNN did not have. Prices give a small clue: roughly $60,000 per H200 in the Northwestern Polytechnical notices, as CNN's totals imply, is the type of figure that suggests grey-market resale rather than a direct Nvidia sale, but that is our arithmetic on CNN's numbers, not a finding.

Each step added buyers, not proof of a pipeline. The common thread is that the controls leave room at the retail edge of China's market, while large, cutting-edge shipments, which are the main worry, are harder to hide.
Does this change what builders can buy? No. These are purchases inside China by blacklisted schools. Cloud and chip availability for ordinary buyers is not affected by this report.
Will Nvidia be penalised? Nothing in the CNN report says so. Rules put the end-user check on suppliers, and enforcement is a Commerce Department matter. No action has been announced.
Why do old chips matter? A100 and A800 are older, but they still train and run useful models. For a university lab that is enough to do real work, which is why the Entity List covers them.

If you resell or procure accelerators, the practical lessons are plain. Check buyers against the Entity List before any sale. Keep an end-user record for each shipment. Be careful with intermediaries whose own supply trail you cannot see. A chip's journey can become a compliance question years later, as these notices show.

We read CNN's full report (published November 19, 2026) and compared it with our earlier coverage of Reuters' November 11 report on Northwestern Polytechnical. We will update this post if the US government or Nvidia responds.
Details are accurate as of November 19, 2026. Procurement records can change or be removed.

On November 20, 2026 Republican Senator Tom Cotton told the Wall Street Journal that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick repeatedly ignored warnings that U.S. AI chips were being smuggled to China before the Nvidia scandal broke. Cotton declined to back Lutnick but stopped short of calling for his firing. This post cites Cotton's October 2025 letter and ties the quote to export-control stakes for GPU buyers.

President Trump told reporters on November 20, 2026 that the United States wants only older chips sold to China and is discussing a comprehensive deal with Beijing. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC the same day that H200 sales policy continues as planned and Jensen Huang was not discussed in latest China talks. This post separates presidential remarks from Bessent's threshold line.

On November 19, 2026 the House Foreign Affairs Committee used its Export Control Reform Act authority to publish Nvidia and AMD export license data for China. It says buyers requested 3.4 million AI chips as of May and Commerce approved more than 879,000. Here is what the committee said, what is still unclear and why it matters.

The report comes as the US seeks to tighten controls on the movement of AI-related hardware into China, including closing loopholes that allow Chinese companies to access computing power through overseas data centres.

The issue is also expected to figure in discussions between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, amid growing competition between the two countries over artificial intelligence and advanced technology.
China, meanwhile, has rejected Washington’s justification for imposing export restrictions.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Beijing opposed what she described as the US misuse of national security concerns to target Chinese institutions through discriminatory lists.
The procurement records reviewed by CNN may not represent the full extent of chip purchases in China.
The commercial database used for the review also does not capture every procurement notice issued by Chinese institutions.
US rules require Nvidia and other chipmakers to assess the end users of products sold overseas and take steps to prevent restricted hardware from reaching prohibited entities.

extraction.body: Nvidia, Export Controls, China, AI Hardware, AI Policy CNN reviewed about 300 procurement notices: at least six US-blacklisted Chinese universities reported buying restricted Nvidia chips. What is confirmed and what is not. Short answer: A CNN review of business records found that at least six Chinese universities on the US Entity List have reported buying restricted Nvidia chips in recent years, including two military-linked schools that reported purchases in the last few months, according to CNN's report of November 19, 2026 . The amounts are small and mostly older chips, bought from obscure Chinese sellers. CNN could not verify delivery, and it is unclear how the sellers got the chips. The finding widens a story we covered earlier this month. Reuters reported on November 11 that one blacklisted school, Northwestern Polytechnical University, bought H200 chips (see our Northwestern Polytechnical coverage ). CNN says the number of universities involved and the full scope of purchases have not been reported before. CNN highlights the cases experts called most notable: "Those are the universities that have tight linkages to the Chinese military," Gregory Allen of Decision Tree Research told CNN, adding that military AI investment would start at such schools. Export-chip control gate behind which a chip rests, representing restricted Nvidia chips reaching blacklisted universities Under Chinese rules, public bodies must publish notices when they make certain purchases. CNN used a commercial database that collects them. It examined nearly 300 records from about 90 buyers: nearly 80% universities, nearly 14% research institutes, and some government agencies. CNN excluded purchases of computing power from overseas data centres, a loophole the Trump administration moved this week to close with new regulations. The limits are significant, and CNN states them. The records are likely incomplete because many institutions only publish notices locally or take them down quickly. The database does not hold every notice. And CNN could not verify that the hardware was delivered in each case. The notices give scant detail on the supply chain or on how the chips would be used. The report does not claim smuggling. It says it is unclear how the sellers acquired the chips. Kate Koren, a former US export control official now at CSIS, offered a possibility: some A100 chips may come "from stockpiles there before the controls were in place," because for a time they were not controlled under US law. A100 sales to China are banned now, but they were widely sold before 2022. She also describes how smuggling networks can work: "very sophisticated shell companies" with multiple hops, currency changes and falsified documents. That is a general description, not a finding about these universities. For a claimed-versus-verified look at one smuggling allegation involving Nvidia executives, see our Muddy Waters GPU diversion explainer . Under a policy set last year after lobbying by Nvidia, the US allows the H200 to be sold to entities in China case by case, with strict requirements to report the end user, per CNN. Experts quoted say officials are highly unlikely to approve sales to a blacklisted university. The Entity List bars shipments of controlled items without federal approval (the license requirements sit in 15 CFR Part 744 of the Export Administration Regulations ), and US rules oblige Nvidia and other suppliers to determine the end user and avoid chips reaching China. So a university on the list buying an H200 through a local reseller does not match an approved sale. It does not tell us whether Nvidia or an authorised distributor did anything wrong. The report does not accuse Nvidia of selling to these buyers. Three points stand out for people who follow AI hardware. Because the whole story rests on these notices, it helps to know what they are. A Chinese public university that buys equipment above a set value must publish a notice, usually on its own procurement page or a government platform. The notice typically names the buyer, the item, the quantity, the price in yuan and the winning supplier. It rarely says where the supplier got the item, who will use it, or whether delivery happened. That is why the same record can support two stories. A cautious reading says a school ordered a chip and a reseller won the order. A stronger reading says restricted hardware reached a military-linked campus. The first is what the notice shows; the second needs proof of delivery and of the chip's path, which CNN did not have. Prices give a small clue: roughly $60,000 per H200 in the Northwestern Polytechnical notices, as CNN's totals imply, is the type of figure that suggests grey-market resale rather than a direct Nvidia sale, but that is our arithmetic on CNN's numbers, not a finding. Each step added buyers, not proof of a pipeline. The common thread is that the controls leave room at the retail edge of China's market, while large, cutting-edge shipments, which are the main worry, are harder to hide. Does this change what builders can buy? No. These are purchases inside China by blacklisted schools. Cloud and chip availability for ordinary buyers is not affected by this report. Will Nvidia be penalised? Nothing in the CNN report says so. Rules put the end-user check on suppliers, and enforcement is a Commerce Department matter. No action has been announced. Why do old chips matter? A100 and A800 are older, but they still train and run useful models. For a university lab that is enough to do real work, which is why the Entity List covers them. If you resell or procure accelerators, the practical lessons are plain. Check buyers against the Entity List before any sale. Keep an end-user record for each shipment. Be careful with intermediaries whose own supply trail you cannot see. A chip's journey can become a compliance question years later, as these notices show. We read CNN's full report (published November 19, 2026) and compared it with our earlier coverage of Reuters' November 11 report on Northwestern Polytechnical. We will update this post if the US government or Nvidia responds. Details are accurate as of November 19, 2026. Procurement records can change or be removed. On November 20, 2026 Republican Senator Tom Cotton told the Wall Street Journal that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick repeatedly ignored warnings that U.S. AI chips were being smuggled to China before the Nvidia scandal broke. Cotton declined to back Lutnick but stopped short of calling for his firing. This post cites Cotton's October 2025 letter and ties the quote to export-control stakes for GPU buyers. President Trump told reporters on November 20, 2026 that the United States wants only older chips sold to China and is discussing a comprehensive deal with Beijing. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC the same day that H200 sales policy continues as planned and Jensen Huang was not discussed in latest China talks. This post separates presidential remarks from Bessent's threshold line. On November 19, 2026 the House Foreign Affairs Committee used its Export Control Reform Act authority to publish Nvidia and AMD export license data for China. It says buyers requested 3.4 million AI chips as of May and Commerce approved more than 879,000. Here is what the committee said, what is still unclear and why it matters.

extraction.body: At least six Chinese universities placed on the US government's Entity List have reported purchasing Nvidia processors subject to American export restrictions, raising questions about the enforcement of Washington's curbs on advanced computing technology. A review of nearly 300 Chinese procurement records by CNN found that the purchases took place over several years, with two universities closely linked to China's military establishment reporting transactions in recent months. extraction.body: West Virginia’s state legislature is responding to a cyberattack that has taken down its website and impacted IT systems. Ann Ali, deputy chief of staff for the House of Delegates, told Recorded Future News that the attack started on Thursday and has continued through Friday. “Upon discovery, the relevant teams immediately took steps to contain the incident and began an investigation with the help of outside cybersecurity specialists,” Ali said. “In connection with the investigation, access to certain Legislature IT systems has been temporarily disabled. However, based on what we know so far, the incident appears to be limited to the Legislature’s computer systems.” She added that no other state agencies or offices are impacted by the cyberattack. An investigation into the incident is ongoing but Ali did not respond to follow-up questions about whether it was a ransomware attack. No hacking groups have taken credit as of Friday. The West Virginia legislature is split between two bodies, a Senate and a House of Delegates with 134 total members representing the state’s 1.7 million residents. Multiple municipalities in the state have dealt with ransomware attacks in recent years, including the cities of Beckley and Westmoreland . Security research firm Comparitech tracked 132 ransomware attacks on government bodies across the U.S. in the third quarter — a 91% increase compared to Q3 last year. At least 41 of the attacks involved U.S. based municipalities, including a major incident impacting Anne Arundel County in Maryland. Ann Ali, deputy chief of staff for the House of Delegates, told Recorded Future News that the attack started on Thursday and has continued through Friday. “Upon discovery, the relevant teams immediately took steps to contain the incident and began an investigation with the help of outside cybersecurity specialists,” Ali said. “In connection with the investigation, access to certain Legislature IT systems has been temporarily disabled. However, based on what we know so far, the incident appears to be limited to the Legislature’s computer systems.” She added that no other state agencies or offices are impacted by the cyberattack. An investigation into the incident is ongoing but Ali did not respond to follow-up questions about whether it was a ransomware attack. No hacking groups have taken credit as of Friday. The West Virginia legislature is split between two bodies, a Senate and a House of Delegates with 134 total members representing the state’s 1.7 million residents. Multiple municipalities in the state have dealt with ransomware attacks in recent years, including the cities of Beckley and Westmoreland . Security research firm Comparitech tracked 132 ransomware attacks on government bodies across the U.S. in the third quarter — a 91% increase compared to Q3 last year. At least 41 of the attacks involved U.S. based municipalities, including a major incident impacting Anne Arundel County in Maryland. sources.title: Trump says only older chips will be sold to China - Cryptopolitan
passages: Trump’s comments came after the US made its chip export rules stricter.
Since early 2025, chips made with 16- or 14-nanometer technology or newer methods have faced restrictions.
These chips are usually seen as AI chips and need US approval before they can be sold to other countries.
President Donald Trump said Friday that China would only be allowed to buy older US chips.
His comments came as chip and AI stocks fell sharply, while Bitcoin dropped 6%.
Trump also said the US was working on “a very comprehensive deal with China” but gave no details or timeline.
“We want only older chips, and we don’t mind if none go.
Samsung also stopped some chip shipments to China while waiting for US approval.
He argued that banning all chip sales would push China to make its own chips.
“In two years, Blackwell will be obsolete,” Trump stated.
Markets were already falling sharply when Trump made the statement.
By early Friday afternoon in New York, the Nasdaq 100 had fallen 3.8% to 25,513, bringing its loss for the week to 9.7%.
Chipmakers were able to avoid the rules previously by showing that their chips had fewer transistors.
The new rule, however, removes this option for chip designers in China and other restricted countries.
According to Reuters , Taiwan’s TSMC stopped taking orders for 16 nanometer and newer chips from some Chinese companies.
Trump also spoke about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who recently resigned after admitting to an affair.
Trump compared Huang to Elon Musk and said he wanted him to apologize and return to Nvidia.
However, Nvidia’s board does not plan to bring Huang back.
Board chairman Harvey Jones said this during Tuesday’s earnings call.

The US has allowed Nvidia to sell its weaker H200 chips to China, but not its more powerful Blackwell chips. “In two years, Blackwell will be obsolete,” Trump stated.
