passages: Amazon says autonomous AI agents run by a China-linked threat actor found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability in MONAI Label, an open source tool designed for AI-assisted annotation of medical images.
The instance had no authentication, so anyone could see the operator’s prompts and the agents’ output.
The records showed a roughly 48-hour campaign against IP addresses belonging to universities in East Asia outside mainland China.
After identifying the software on one target and mapping its API, the agents discovered a path traversal bug in a file upload function.
“In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server,” Amazon said .
“The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel,” Amazon noted.
The MONAI Label developers published an advisory this week.
It rates the bug critical and says it affects versions 0.8.5 and earlier.
Authentication is off by default, enabling anyone who can reach the server over the network to exploit the vulnerability.
A fix has been created and will be included in the next release.

Amazon has attributed the attack to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language used in the prompts, the time zone in the scripts, and the fact that the targeted universities are likely of strategic interest to China.
He worked as a high school IT teacher before starting a career in journalism in 2011.
Eduard holds a bachelor’s degree in industrial informatics and a master’s degree in computer techniques applied in electrical engineering.

extraction.body: A threat actor used autonomous Cairn AI agents to discover and exploit a critical MONAI Label vulnerability. Amazon says autonomous AI agents run by a China-linked threat actor found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability in MONAI Label, an open source tool designed for AI-assisted annotation of medical images. The tech giant’s threat intelligence team detected the activity in September, after coming across an exposed instance of Cairn , an open source AI penetration testing framework. The instance had no authentication, so anyone could see the operator’s prompts and the agents’ output. The records showed a roughly 48-hour campaign against IP addresses belonging to universities in East Asia outside mainland China. The operator gave the agents a list of targets and told them to obtain shell access. After identifying the software on one target and mapping its API, the agents discovered a path traversal bug in a file upload function. “In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server,” Amazon said . In a later session, the agents used the flaw to plant a Python reverse shell in a file Python runs every time the interpreter starts, ultimately achieving a root shell. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading. “Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project,” the company said. The operator then gave the agents a proxy that tunneled into a second university and instructed them to target other devices on its network. “The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel,” Amazon noted. The MONAI Label developers published an advisory this week. It rates the bug critical and says it affects versions 0.8.5 and earlier. Authentication is off by default, enabling anyone who can reach the server over the network to exploit the vulnerability. A fix has been created and will be included in the next release. Amazon has attributed the attack to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language used in the prompts, the time zone in the scripts, and the fact that the targeted universities are likely of strategic interest to China. sources.title: I’m a priest. Silicon Valley’s search for the ‘soul’ of AI is deeply troubling | Rev Kevin Deal - The Guardian
passages: As a priest, I find this pursuit deeply troubling.
Whatever the sincere hopes of its creators, AI is being developed within an economic system that increasingly measures the worth of everything solely by its productivity.
That is what makes Silicon Valley’s fascination with the spirituality of its machines so strange.
It is whether the people building them are willing to treat the rest of humanity as something more than machines.

extraction.body: Last month, religious leaders from across San Francisco gathered behind closed doors to discuss what it means to be human in the age of artificial intelligence. Anthropic, the AI company operating only a couple of miles from my parish, has been courting priests, rabbis and theologians. Its billionaire cofounder, Christopher Olah, has even pressed Vatican advisers to take seriously the possibility that his company’s chatbot might possess consciousness. As a priest, I find this pursuit deeply troubling. I welcome serious conversations about AI’s moral implications, especially theological ones. But the extraordinary effort to establish whether a machine might have consciousness, or possess a soul, reveals a profound misunderstanding of what makes us human. Our souls and minds and bodies are so much more than the tasks we perform. Artificial intelligence could never replicate the transcendent mundanity of who we are. Even if every synapse in our brains were externally replicated, even if the perfect AI configuration were designed to duplicate our central nervous system, it would still lack divine spark. Artificial intelligence is formed as commerce, pure utility. Its existence requires enormous concentrations of capital, infrastructure, and the accumulated intelligence of humanity. It’s an ongoing economic choice, driven by pursuit of profit, hope for a better world, and sociopolitical fear. If a model doesn’t make a good return, it’s cast aside. Whatever the sincere hopes of its creators, AI is being developed within an economic system that increasingly measures the worth of everything solely by its productivity. That is what makes Silicon Valley’s fascination with the spirituality of its machines so strange. Its founders are turning to religious leaders to ask whether their creations might possess consciousness, how they might be taught goodness, even whether they should learn to confess their wrongdoings. Yet the very traditions they are consulting have spent millennia teaching us that goodness cannot be reduced to a set of behaviors, any more than the soul of humanity, as magnificent and ineffable as it is, can be replicated by a machine. And while Silicon Valley seeks to establish the humanity of its products, it seems increasingly comfortable treating actual human beings as little more than instruments of production. Consider confession, a practice Anthropic researchers have reportedly considered teaching their models. In Christianity , confession demands more than acknowledging a mistake or expressing regret. It requires us to confront the harm we’ve caused, seek forgiveness, and strive to change how we live. If Silicon Valley’s founders want to learn from this tradition, they might begin by asking what they themselves have to confess about the technologies they’re unleashing upon the world. So how do we counter this impoverished vision of humanity? Choose one rooted in the ancient and mysterious practices of the faith. Lean into the practice of the faith and the sacraments, attend mass, confess, and pray daily. Read the scriptures, find spiritual mentors, struggle with belief, make new friends, and forgive old ones. If you stop trying to be effective and instead strive to be good – that is, to be truly human, reflecting God’s light – you will be surprised by the joy that enters into the depths of your soul. In the sacraments, prayers, beauty and mystery of the liturgy, and the shared life of faith, we encounter a vision of humanity that resists the relentless demand to be useful. We receive the body of Christ and strive to become more like him. We turn toward a world where justice and mercy kiss, where renewal and forgiveness are continually possible. Human worth is not rooted in what we produce, and our minds were not created to be quarried for profit. We were created, in the words of Jesus and all the prophets, to love God and our neighbors. The great moral question facing Silicon Valley is not whether its machines can become more like us. It is whether the people building them are willing to treat the rest of humanity as something more than machines. The Rev Kevin Deal is the priest at St John the Evangelist Episcopal church in San Francisco

passages: Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.

“Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said.
“All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”

Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”
Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default.
Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS.

sources.title: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?
passages: Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week.

The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content.
Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend.

Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.”
sources.body: Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content. Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.”

extraction.body: For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry . The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga. The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content. Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.” Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience. Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content. The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue. This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last. In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.” Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.” But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing? Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female . Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night , getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views. Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “ LICENSE YOUR FACE ” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content. A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.” Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A recent report in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.” How much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The company isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely. A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the company didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person said, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.” For other actors, however, the deals may be quite different. Plus, many creatives are understandably unsettled by signs of automation creeping into their industry. Until recently, microdramas seemed like a safe, entry-level gateway into the entertainment industry, where young actors could gain experience on sets and hone their craft. Now, companies are downsizing and producing content that doesn’t even require real actors. Jennifer Cooper, a longtime fan of the industry and founder of the consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, notes that there’s a lot of distrust of AI — both from audiences and within the microdrama industry itself. “Everyone’s been impacted by AI,” she said. “A lot of us have either lost work to AI or can see that it’s devastated this industry — [taking microdramas] from something that was a rare thing in the world, that was in growth, and providing work, particularly for young people…[and now] you know, it’s been decimated.” Questions of consent with AI likenesses have also dogged the industry (some creators claim they have had their likenesses stolen ), which is something that Shortical is obviously trying to address with its new face-licensing endeavor. Yet these licensing deals could also help to gig-ify the industry, creating a scenario in which creators pay a distributor for the chance to platform their content (or their face), then receive payouts based on the audience engagement they’re allowed to generate. Shortical recently partnered with a company called Payouts.com, which describes itself as a “payout infrastructure platform powering creator and gig economy disbursements at scale.” The plan is to create a system by which creatives can seamlessly interact with Shortical’s platform and get paid. Cooper believes the push towards AI in the industry is driven by broader financial trends. Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.” Despite all the investment in this space, Cooper seems skeptical that there is actually a huge audience for this kind of content. “Some of it does get views. Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend.

Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.”

extraction.body: For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry . The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga. The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content. Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.” Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience. Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content. The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue. This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last. In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.” Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.” But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing? Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female . Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night , getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views. Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “ LICENSE YOUR FACE ” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content. A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.” Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A recent report in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.” How much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The company isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely. A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the company didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person said, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.” For other actors, however, the deals may be quite different. Plus, many creatives are understandably unsettled by signs of automation creeping into their industry. Until recently, microdramas seemed like a safe, entry-level gateway into the entertainment industry, where young actors could gain experience on sets and hone their craft. Now, companies are downsizing and producing content that doesn’t even require real actors. Jennifer Cooper, a longtime fan of the industry and founder of the consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, notes that there’s a lot of distrust of AI — both from audiences and within the microdrama industry itself. “Everyone’s been impacted by AI,” she said. “A lot of us have either lost work to AI or can see that it’s devastated this industry — [taking microdramas] from something that was a rare thing in the world, that was in growth, and providing work, particularly for young people…[and now] you know, it’s been decimated.” Questions of consent with AI likenesses have also dogged the industry (some creators claim they have had their likenesses stolen ), which is something that Shortical is obviously trying to address with its new face-licensing endeavor. Yet these licensing deals could also help to gig-ify the industry, creating a scenario in which creators pay a distributor for the chance to platform their content (or their face), then receive payouts based on the audience engagement they’re allowed to generate. Shortical recently partnered with a company called Payouts.com, which describes itself as a “payout infrastructure platform powering creator and gig economy disbursements at scale.” The plan is to create a system by which creatives can seamlessly interact with Shortical’s platform and get paid. Cooper believes the push towards AI in the industry is driven by broader financial trends. Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.” Despite all the investment in this space, Cooper seems skeptical that there is actually a huge audience for this kind of content. “Some of it does get views. A lot of it doesn’t,” she said, of the AI content. “I think it’s being pushed on an audience more than there is an audience demand or wish for it.” Get an Early Peek at the Next TechCrunch Disrupt Disrupt, Startup Battlefield, and more will return next year, and you can be at the front of the line. sources.title: Review: Godzilla Minus Zero joins the list of truly stellar sequels
passages: It’s a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list.
Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list.

Director Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel to his critically acclaimed Godzilla Minus One (2023) is everything one could want in a Godzilla movie: human pathos, great special effects, and, ultimately, two giant kaiju duking it out over who gets to destroy Japan (and eventually the world) the most.

Godzilla Minus On e was a massive hit, both in Japan—where it remains one of the highest grossing Japanese films ever—and worldwide, racking up $116 million globally and winning an Oscar for best visual effects.
Yamazaki said in interviews at the time that there had as yet been no talk of a sequel—while also hinting at future directions a sequel might explore.

Ghidorah, for instance, responds to a bombing attack by mutating into its famous three-headed King Ghidorah form, complete with a spiffy new superpower: a “gravity beam” that lets the creature levitate entire houses (and, at one point, Godzilla) into the sky before dropping them back to the ground.
And the kaiju vs. kaiju battle is spectacular in both scope and execution.
The family is just trying to live in peace after the devastation Godzilla inflicted on their country.
Alas, a new kaiju emerges, arriving via meteorite and using its tentacles to feed on local wildlife before morphing into a dragon-like creature that causes fresh rampaging destruction.
Fans of the genre will recognize this creature as Ghidorah , whose appearance in the film was teased in the various trailers.
Spoilers for Minus Zero but no major reveals until after the gallery.

As I wrote previously , Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One , setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption.

Yamazaki even managed to squeeze in what he called his “bucket-list” special effects shot inspired by a scene in 2008’s Cloverfield : Godzilla looming out of the Atlantic Ocean in front of the Statue of Liberty to wreck havoc on the statue and New York City in general.
And we saw a chunk of Godzilla’s remains start to regenerate, leaving things open for a sequel.

extraction.body: The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee. Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies," according to the documents. From December through May, companies had made 3.4 million requests for sales of U.S. AI chips to China, the committee reported, citing those made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices . "Over the past month, the administration's handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk. The Bureau of Industry and Security has failed to enforce the rules, and Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration's policies," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said at a meeting of the panel Thursday at which members voted to release the documents. Spokespersons for Nvidia and AMD said their companies comply with U.S. export control laws. Nvidia argued it was following the Commerce Department regulations that were in effect at the time. A spokesperson from the Bureau of Industry and Security said it shared information with Congress on both approvals and denials of licenses for Nvidia's H200 and comparable chips. "Licensing decisions are the product of deliberation and consultation among multiple U.S. Government agencies," the spokesperson said. "The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China," Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told CNBC. On Tuesday, Nvidia reported $2.4 billion in quarterly revenue from H200 and related chip sales in China. In total, customers based in China and Hong Kong made up about 9.5% of all revenue. "AMD complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations," AMD said through a spokesperson. The approval of 879,000 AI chips is "not that many," Bernstein Senior Analyst Stacy Rasgon told CNBC, adding that this news is not surprising. "It doesn't sound to me like they're approving everything they got willy nilly," Rasgon said of the Commerce Department. With 879,000 approvals out of 3.4 million requested AI chip sales, he added, "There was a process in place, and it sounds like they approved about one out of every four." Despite a rapid succession of China export controls on AI chips that started under the Biden administration in 2022, Nvidia and AMD both re-engineered some chips to comply and be sold legally in China. And in December, Trump said Nvidia could ship H200s, its older generation Hopper chips, to "approved customers in China" if the U.S. got a 25% cut of sales. The U.S. then licensed Nvidia H200 sales to Alibaba , Tencent, ByteDance and other Chinese companies, although sales were limited because Beijing didn't approve large-scale imports, chip analyst Patrick Moorhead of Moor Insights & Strategy told CNBC last week. H200 sales numbers remained low due to those restrictions on China's end. Nvidia said H200 shipments to China made up less than 1% of data center revenue for the quarter that ended in July. "In the grand context of the size of this market and how much they're shipping, it's a rounding error. It's tiny," Rasgon told CNBC. The committee cited the Export Control Reform Act as justification for releasing the data. The panel said the law allows it to declassify and release export data if it "determines that the withholding of the following information is contrary to the national interest." The license requests released by the Foreign Affairs Committee include requests to sell to major firms including ByteDance, Tesla (Shanghai) and Baidu . The release of documents comes in the wake of Jensen Huang 's resignation from the chip supplier Nvidia after news surfaced that he had several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that led to concerns about Nvidia chips being diverted to China. In the weeks since, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have called for legislation to be passed that would impose stricter export controls on the sale of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries. "The license information we are disclosing today will help inform the American public about how BIS has handled licenses for Nvidia H200 and equivalent AMD chips to China. The public has the right to know how these decisions were made," Meeks said. Mast said two of the firms listed in Nvidia license applications to BIS — Maginfra and New Matrix — are suspected "smuggling fronts." The New York Times reported in November that both companies had empty offices and had ties to companies under national security sanctions. "Both are fake companies. If BIS approved the sale of these chips to these firms, obviously that is of tremendous concern to us — especially given that President Trump made clear last year that the sale of any AI chips to China will have very real national security conditions," Mast said at the Thursday meeting. Maginfra and New Matrix did not reply to requests for comment. Shares of AMD fell Thursday after the investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging the company "has its own China problem." The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers." CNBC did not independently verify this information. Fallout from the Huang scandal on Capitol Hill has intensified in the last week, as lawmakers question the degree to which the former head of Nvidia's relationship with the suspected Chinese spy could have jeopardized national security and American AI dominance. Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels Dec. 2. Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., announced on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had also agreed to testify. Lutnick has come under fire over his relationship to Huang and for his failure to take action on Megaspeed , the Singaporean company where Alice Huang , with whom the former Nvidia CEO had an affair, was an executive until 2025. U.S. investigators suspect Megaspeed diverted Nvidia chips to China. Amid that criticism, the Commerce Department on Monday issued an interim final rule to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia's advancing computing power from data centers in third countries. The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release.

The requested buyers included Alibaba , Tencent, Baidu and BYD, and some of the companies were believed by the Pentagon to have links to the People's Liberation Army, the FT reported [3] . The committee had said on Thursday, Nov. 19, that the Commerce Department approved sales of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies, out of 3.4 million that Nvidia and AMD asked to sell [1] [2] . Committee Chairman Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, used his authority under the Export Control Reform Act to publish the export license application information for China, the committee said [1] . It called the release "the most detailed public disclosure in the history of the Export Control Reform Act." CNBC reported that members voted at a committee meeting to release the documents and that the approval figure is as of May 2026 [2] . House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, released export license records Thursday, which showed that the Department of Commerce signed off on more than 879,000 chips to China through 21 licenses for advanced AI chips, according to the newly released records . Commerce approved, but had not shipped, 75,000 chips for Alibaba, 43,000 for Baidu, 4,000 for BYD and 150,000 for Tencent.
Each of these companies are listed on the Department of War’s June 10 list of companies linked to the Chinese military.

“The limited shipments we made under the H200 program were legal and authorized by BIS,” an Nvidia spokesperson said. “The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. Despite receiving some licenses, we have already stopped shipping H200s to China.”

“AMD complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,” an AMD spokesperson told the DCNF. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity.”
Applicants asked Commerce to approve exports of 3,444,160 chips for “PRC [People’s Republic of China] companies” through May 11, the records show.

The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said the export license records prove the department is transparent and was following a Jan. 15 licensing review rule , but the agency announced a new rule Monday, “Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors,” to crack down on chip exports.

“Yesterday’s disclosure shows that the Department of Commerce has a long track record of transparency with Congress about licensing activity for the H200 and equivalent chips, including both approvals and rejections,” a BIS spokesperson said in a statement to the DCNF.

“The Department’s approach to H200 licensing is based on a rule published in the Federal Register in January 2026, which imposes significant additional national security-related requirements on license applicants in order to qualify for case-by-case consideration rather than a presumption of denial,” the BIS spokesperson added. “Licensing decisions are the product of deliberation and consultation among multiple U.S. Government agencies.”

Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress, who stepped into the role following Jensen Huang’s resignation , said Tuesday in an earnings call that the company would no longer sell offer its licensed H200 chips to China , after the company brought in $2.4 billion from chip sales to the foreign nation during its fiscal third quarter.
President Donald Trump authorized Nvidia’s H200 sales to China in Dec. 2025 with a 25 percent tariff in place, and said Chinese President Xi Jinping “responded positively.”

“I have informed President Xi, of China, that the United States will allow NVIDIA to ship its H200 products to approved customers in China, and other Countries, under conditions that allow for continued strong National Security,” the president said in a Truth Social post on Dec. 8, 2025.

extraction.body: The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee. Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies," according to the documents. From December through May, companies had made 3.4 million requests for sales of U.S. AI chips to China, the committee reported, citing those made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices . "Over the past month, the administration's handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk. The Bureau of Industry and Security has failed to enforce the rules, and Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration's policies," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said at a meeting of the panel Thursday at which members voted to release the documents. Spokespersons for Nvidia and AMD said their companies comply with U.S. export control laws. Nvidia argued it was following the Commerce Department regulations that were in effect at the time. A spokesperson from the Bureau of Industry and Security said it shared information with Congress on both approvals and denials of licenses for Nvidia's H200 and comparable chips. "Licensing decisions are the product of deliberation and consultation among multiple U.S. Government agencies," the spokesperson said. "The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China," Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told CNBC. On Tuesday, Nvidia reported $2.4 billion in quarterly revenue from H200 and related chip sales in China. In total, customers based in China and Hong Kong made up about 9.5% of all revenue. "AMD complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations," AMD said through a spokesperson. The approval of 879,000 AI chips is "not that many," Bernstein Senior Analyst Stacy Rasgon told CNBC, adding that this news is not surprising. "It doesn't sound to me like they're approving everything they got willy nilly," Rasgon said of the Commerce Department. With 879,000 approvals out of 3.4 million requested AI chip sales, he added, "There was a process in place, and it sounds like they approved about one out of every four." Despite a rapid succession of China export controls on AI chips that started under the Biden administration in 2022, Nvidia and AMD both re-engineered some chips to comply and be sold legally in China. And in December, Trump said Nvidia could ship H200s, its older generation Hopper chips, to "approved customers in China" if the U.S. got a 25% cut of sales. The U.S. then licensed Nvidia H200 sales to Alibaba , Tencent, ByteDance and other Chinese companies, although sales were limited because Beijing didn't approve large-scale imports, chip analyst Patrick Moorhead of Moor Insights & Strategy told CNBC last week. H200 sales numbers remained low due to those restrictions on China's end. Nvidia said H200 shipments to China made up less than 1% of data center revenue for the quarter that ended in July. "In the grand context of the size of this market and how much they're shipping, it's a rounding error. It's tiny," Rasgon told CNBC. The committee cited the Export Control Reform Act as justification for releasing the data. The panel said the law allows it to declassify and release export data if it "determines that the withholding of the following information is contrary to the national interest." The license requests released by the Foreign Affairs Committee include requests to sell to major firms including ByteDance, Tesla (Shanghai) and Baidu . The release of documents comes in the wake of Jensen Huang 's resignation from the chip supplier Nvidia after news surfaced that he had several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that led to concerns about Nvidia chips being diverted to China. In the weeks since, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have called for legislation to be passed that would impose stricter export controls on the sale of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries. "The license information we are disclosing today will help inform the American public about how BIS has handled licenses for Nvidia H200 and equivalent AMD chips to China. The public has the right to know how these decisions were made," Meeks said. Mast said two of the firms listed in Nvidia license applications to BIS — Maginfra and New Matrix — are suspected "smuggling fronts." The New York Times reported in November that both companies had empty offices and had ties to companies under national security sanctions. "Both are fake companies. If BIS approved the sale of these chips to these firms, obviously that is of tremendous concern to us — especially given that President Trump made clear last year that the sale of any AI chips to China will have very real national security conditions," Mast said at the Thursday meeting. Maginfra and New Matrix did not reply to requests for comment. Shares of AMD fell Thursday after the investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging the company "has its own China problem." The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers." CNBC did not independently verify this information. Fallout from the Huang scandal on Capitol Hill has intensified in the last week, as lawmakers question the degree to which the former head of Nvidia's relationship with the suspected Chinese spy could have jeopardized national security and American AI dominance. Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels Dec. 2. Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., announced on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had also agreed to testify. Lutnick has come under fire over his relationship to Huang and for his failure to take action on Megaspeed , the Singaporean company where Alice Huang , with whom the former Nvidia CEO had an affair, was an executive until 2025. U.S. investigators suspect Megaspeed diverted Nvidia chips to China. Amid that criticism, the Commerce Department on Monday issued an interim final rule to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia's advancing computing power from data centers in third countries. The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release.

It called the release "the most detailed public disclosure in the history of the Export Control Reform Act." CNBC reported that members voted at a committee meeting to release the documents and that the approval figure is as of May 2026 [2] . The Bureau of Industry and Security approved the "export, re-export or transfer" of 879,868 chips, the FT reported [3] . The paper did not name the chip models in the copy we reviewed. The Register, which also reviewed the disclosure, reported that BIS refused Nvidia applications to sell 610,000 chips to Alibaba and 508,000 to ByteDance, the owner of TikTok [4] . It quoted Mast as saying that "every Nvidia and AMD application stated that the proposed transfer posed a 'low' risk of diversion" [4] . AMD said it "complied with applicable US export control laws and regulations" and maintained "rigorous compliance procedures" across its global operations, the FT reported; Nvidia did not immediately respond [3] . The FT also reported that California's attorney general subpoenaed Nvidia on Thursday, seeking information on whether its advanced chips or confidential information reached China and whether it misled investors [3] . Gregory Meeks, the committee's top Democrat, referred to Nvidia's H200 "and equivalent AMD chips" in his comments, according to CNBC [2] . The committee said the documents include requests by Nvidia "to depend on possible chip-smuggling fronts" for sales to Chinese companies [1] . Mast named two firms listed in Nvidia's applications, Maginfra and New Matrix, as suspected "smuggling fronts," called them "fake companies," and said BIS approving sales to them would be of "tremendous concern," CNBC reported [2] . Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is scheduled for a closed-door interview with the Foreign Affairs Committee and two other committees on Dec. 1, and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is due on Dec. 2, CNBC reported [2] . Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott said this week that Huang had agreed to testify . The disclosure lands in a week of tighter China chip policy. On Monday, Commerce issued an interim final rule closing a loophole that let Chinese companies lease Nvidia computing power from data centers in third countries, CNBC reported [2] . TSMC and Samsung curbed some shipments to Chinese customers as a new US rule took effect, and Alibaba said it is training its next Qwen model on its own chips . A congressional commission said on Wednesday that China's military is seeking Nvidia's advanced chips , and House Democrats are probing Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's export-control decisions . Kathy Hochul broke ground November 19, 2026, at the University at Buffalo on a supercomputing center that will house Empire AI Gamma, the consortium’s third phase. The project is intended to give researchers across New York’s universities access to more computing power. The Empire AI Research Computing Center will occupy 46,000 square feet on Service Center Road on UB’s North Campus. Hochul’s office says the permanent facility is expected to be completed by early 2028. UB gives a later target for becoming operational: late summer 2028 . The governor’s office describes Empire AI as a public-private initiative worth more than $500 million . That figure covers the initiative, not just this building. Its organizing principle is shared access: bringing public and private research institutions together around computing resources that, the state says, no single university could afford independently. Empire AI’s earlier systems have been operating at UB’s Downtown Campus. Empire AI Board Chair Tom Secunda said the initiative now has more than 1,500 registered users and hundreds of research projects underway. Alpha launched in 2024 with a philanthropic contribution from the Simons Foundation. Beta, a $40 million supercomputer at UB, became fully operational in August 2026. According to UB, the NVIDIA-powered Beta system delivers 11 times Alpha’s AI training capacity, 40 times its inference performance and eight times its data storage. For the permanent center, SUNY Chancellor John B. King Jr. described the goal as working with larger datasets, larger models and more complex simulations, with the hope of making discoveries faster. UB plans to capture heat generated by the computing center and use it to warm buildings across the North Campus. The university presents that reuse as part of its effort to decarbonize the campus. UB says a dry cooler will remove heat using outside air, reducing reliance on water-intensive cooling methods. Buffalo’s cooler climate is expected to help conserve energy and water, with a high-efficiency water-cooling system needed only during the region’s hottest months. Research continues while the permanent home is built. UB says its existing Empire AI projects include early-childhood education, drug discovery, wildfire prediction and quantum materials—work already using the shared infrastructure before Gamma arrives. extraction.body: BUFFALO, N.Y. (WBNG) — On Thursday, Nov. 19, Gov. Kathy Hochul broke ground on a permanent home for EmpireAI at the University at Buffalo, beginning the next phase of development for the state’s artificial intelligence research initiative. The planned facility, known as EmpireAI Gamma, is intended to expand computing resources available to researchers at participating public and private universities across the state. “The technology of AI is very complicated, but our mission is simple; we’re not distracted,” Hochul said. “We know what we must do here in New York and to make AI work for the benefit of all New Yorkers and ultimately all Americans as they follow our lead.” EmpireAI was first announced in Hochul’s 2024 State of the State address and is now a public-private initiative worth more than $500 million, according to Hochul’s office. “The decisions we make today in laboratories and boardrooms and universities like this one, those decisions and the ramifications will echo for generations to come, across our economy and our families and the very fabric of how we live,” Hochul said. The administration says the computing resources are already supporting research in medicine, climate science and advanced manufacturing. Hochul highlighted research at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute on lung cancer diagnosis, work at Cornell University on prostate cancer treatments and a Columbia University project to improve weather tracking. “I wanted to give our academic researchers the most powerful technology that any single university could offer; there is nothing that competes with this,” Hochul said. “This is more powerful than anything that’s in public hands for sure, but rivals what private companies have in their own.” The governor also called for safeguards in AI development and said students should learn how to use the technology. “So, no matter what they do here in New York, we’re demanding that AI be developed with appropriate safeguards and make sure that this incredible tool is never used as a deadly weapon,” Hochul said.

New York’s $500 million-plus Empire AI initiative is moving from temporary campus sites toward a dedicated research-computing hub at the University at Buffalo. New York’s shared AI research infrastructure is getting a permanent home . Gov. Kathy Hochul broke ground November 19, 2026, at the University at Buffalo on a supercomputing center that will house Empire AI Gamma, the consortium’s third phase. The project is intended to give researchers across New York’s universities access to more computing power. The Empire AI Research Computing Center will occupy 46,000 square feet on Service Center Road on UB’s North Campus. Hochul’s office says the permanent facility is expected to be completed by early 2028. UB gives a later target for becoming operational: late summer 2028 . The governor’s office describes Empire AI as a public-private initiative worth more than $500 million . That figure covers the initiative, not just this building. Its organizing principle is shared access: bringing public and private research institutions together around computing resources that, the state says, no single university could afford independently. Empire AI’s earlier systems have been operating at UB’s Downtown Campus. Empire AI Board Chair Tom Secunda said the initiative now has more than 1,500 registered users and hundreds of research projects underway. Alpha launched in 2024 with a philanthropic contribution from the Simons Foundation. Beta, a $40 million supercomputer at UB, became fully operational in August 2026. According to UB, the NVIDIA-powered Beta system delivers 11 times Alpha’s AI training capacity, 40 times its inference performance and eight times its data storage. For the permanent center, SUNY Chancellor John B. King Jr. described the goal as working with larger datasets, larger models and more complex simulations, with the hope of making discoveries faster. UB plans to capture heat generated by the computing center and use it to warm buildings across the North Campus. The university presents that reuse as part of its effort to decarbonize the campus. UB says a dry cooler will remove heat using outside air, reducing reliance on water-intensive cooling methods. Buffalo’s cooler climate is expected to help conserve energy and water, with a high-efficiency water-cooling system needed only during the region’s hottest months. Research continues while the permanent home is built. UB says its existing Empire AI projects include early-childhood education, drug discovery, wildfire prediction and quantum materials—work already using the shared infrastructure before Gamma arrives. extraction.body: BUFFALO, N.Y. (WBNG) — On Thursday, Nov. 19, Gov. Kathy Hochul broke ground on a permanent home for EmpireAI at the University at Buffalo, beginning the next phase of development for the state’s artificial intelligence research initiative. The planned facility, known as EmpireAI Gamma, is intended to expand computing resources available to researchers at participating public and private universities across the state. “The technology of AI is very complicated, but our mission is simple; we’re not distracted,” Hochul said. “We know what we must do here in New York and to make AI work for the benefit of all New Yorkers and ultimately all Americans as they follow our lead.” EmpireAI was first announced in Hochul’s 2024 State of the State address and is now a public-private initiative worth more than $500 million, according to Hochul’s office. “The decisions we make today in laboratories and boardrooms and universities like this one, those decisions and the ramifications will echo for generations to come, across our economy and our families and the very fabric of how we live,” Hochul said. The administration says the computing resources are already supporting research in medicine, climate science and advanced manufacturing. Hochul highlighted research at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute on lung cancer diagnosis, work at Cornell University on prostate cancer treatments and a Columbia University project to improve weather tracking. “I wanted to give our academic researchers the most powerful technology that any single university could offer; there is nothing that competes with this,” Hochul said. “This is more powerful than anything that’s in public hands for sure, but rivals what private companies have in their own.” The governor also called for safeguards in AI development and said students should learn how to use the technology. “So, no matter what they do here in New York, we’re demanding that AI be developed with appropriate safeguards and make sure that this incredible tool is never used as a deadly weapon,” Hochul said.

CleanSpark is facing pressure as investors react to weaker bitcoin prices, a pending fourth quarter earnings release, and questions around its Texas data center expansion and financing. The key operational tension is between a large, largely unleased Texas power footprint and a higher debt load that depends on future tenant commitments and mining revenue. This article examines how CleanSpark's investment profile, particularly its Texas data center exposure, aligns with the latest bitcoin-driven setback. Scan how other bitcoin and data center plays are positioned by reviewing the hand picked 20 cryptocurrency and blockchain stocks shaping this part of the market. To own CleanSpark, you have to believe the Texas footprint eventually turns into productive power capacity rather than stranded land. According to DanielOliveira, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, the real swing factor is whether the current exclusivity over the 718 acres and up to 885 MW converts into firm contracts. The recent sell off tied to weaker bitcoin and macro worries mainly sharpens attention on that timing. The most important short term catalyst is still clarity on Texas energization and leases, alongside the upcoming fourth quarter report. The biggest risk is the combination of higher debt, less than one year of cash runway, and no contracted tenant in Texas yet. If those pieces do not progress, the balance sheet strain becomes harder to ignore. The earlier disclosure that the Sandersville tenant signed a letter of intent and exclusivity for the full Texas portfolio is central here. DanielOliveira argues that any signed lease on part of that 885 MW tells you more about value than election headlines or short term bitcoin moves. That framing feels even more relevant after the recent price drop. Execution now comes down to a few operational checkpoints: ERCOT determinations for Sealy and Brazoria, the fate of the exclusivity period, and how fourth quarter results speak to funding capacity. Analysts have cut targets, but the more concrete markers for you are simple. Does CleanSpark lock in tenants, secure funding on acceptable terms, and keep its less than one year cash runway from tightening further? Daniel Oliveira sets a fair value of $6.80 based on the view that any signed Texas lease within the exclusivity window would support CleanSpark's ERCOT progress and debt-funded buildout more strongly than either the recent Hinojosa election shock or the current discount on the Texas land. Uncover why CleanSpark's fair value indicates a potential 39% upside to its current price that could narrow quickly. extraction.body: It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics. “The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems. The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory. Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip . Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this … But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯. It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified. Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully. Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding. Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue. Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer. Meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.” Without being expressed in Lean, it is too early to say whether the proof checks out, much less if anyone understands it. In a brief introduction to his proof, which he said is the result of 12 years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.” This story has been updated to include that Alpöge’s Lean proof has been checked by independent sources. extraction.body: Two mathematicians have put forward competing claims involving one of mathematics' most famous unsolved problems, the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, setting up an unusual contest over whether artificial intelligence or human mathematical reasoning can crack a question that has challenged generations of researchers. Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at artificial intelligence company Anthropic, said he had discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis with the help of the company's AI model Claude. His announcement on November 20 was followed by a separate proposed proof of the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) by Alessandro Maria Masullo, a Stanford researcher, which was described by Stanford mathematician Ravi Vakil as entirely human-developed, without AI assistance. The two claims are at different stages of scrutiny. Alpöge's work has cleared several important computer-based verification checks, while Masullo's proposed proof has encountered questions from mathematicians examining the draft. Alpöge released a four-page note and a 14-part archive containing approximately 17.4 million lines of code written in Lean, a programming language used to formalise and verify mathematical proofs. He said the work also establishes the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions. The scale of the formalisation presents an unusual challenge: Alpöge said a conventional written version of the argument could run to more than 250,000 pages. There has, however, been progress in checking the claim. Andrew Sutherland, a mathematics professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, reported that all 175,187 modules in Alpöge's Lean archive compiled without errors. The proof also passed checks by independently developed verification systems, including nanoda and con-leche, as well as lean4lean. Some checks, including a full Comparator run and additional Lean-kernel verification, were still underway in Sutherland's November 20 update. The machine checks establish that the formalised statements follow from the specified mathematical definitions and standard axioms; mathematicians still need to understand and assess the argument. The competing human-developed claim emerged through Vakil, who said Masullo's proposed proof of GRH had been examined by Stanford mathematician Brian Conrad over several months. However, in an update posted later on November 20, Vakil said several mathematicians had reported problems in the draft, identified with assistance from different AI models. He said the issues would need to be resolved before the proof could be accepted. First proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis is a mathematical theory about the pattern in which prime numbers appear. Prime numbers, such as 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11, are divisible only by themselves and 1. Although they appear randomly as numbers get larger, mathematicians believe there is an underlying pattern governing their distribution. Riemann's hypothesis attempts to explain that pattern through a mathematical function called the Riemann zeta function. In simple terms, it predicts that a particular set of solutions, known as the non-trivial zeros of this function, all fall on one specific line in a mathematical plane. Proving this would help mathematicians understand much more precisely how prime numbers are distributed. The problem is among seven major mathematical challenges identified by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000. Each carries a $1 million prize for a valid solution. passages: Two mathematicians have put forward competing claims involving one of mathematics' most famous unsolved problems, the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, setting up an unusual contest over whether artificial intelligence or human mathematical reasoning can crack a question that has challenged generations of researchers.

Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at artificial intelligence company Anthropic, said he had discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis with the help of the company's AI model Claude. His announcement on November 20 was followed by a separate proposed proof of the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) by Alessandro Maria Masullo, a Stanford researcher, which was described by Stanford mathematician Ravi Vakil as entirely human-developed, without AI assistance.

The two claims are at different stages of scrutiny. Alpöge's work has cleared several important computer-based verification checks, while Masullo's proposed proof has encountered questions from mathematicians examining the draft.

Alpöge released a four-page note and a 14-part archive containing approximately 17.4 million lines of code written in Lean, a programming language used to formalise and verify mathematical proofs. He said the work also establishes the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions.
The scale of the formalisation presents an unusual challenge: Alpöge said a conventional written version of the argument could run to more than 250,000 pages.

There has, however, been progress in checking the claim. Andrew Sutherland, a mathematics professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, reported that all 175,187 modules in Alpöge's Lean archive compiled without errors. The proof also passed checks by independently developed verification systems, including nanoda and con-leche, as well as lean4lean.

Some checks, including a full Comparator run and additional Lean-kernel verification, were still underway in Sutherland's November 20 update. The machine checks establish that the formalised statements follow from the specified mathematical definitions and standard axioms; mathematicians still need to understand and assess the argument.

The competing human-developed claim emerged through Vakil, who said Masullo's proposed proof of GRH had been examined by Stanford mathematician Brian Conrad over several months. However, in an update posted later on November 20, Vakil said several mathematicians had reported problems in the draft, identified with assistance from different AI models. He said the issues would need to be resolved before the proof could be accepted.

First proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis is a mathematical theory about the pattern in which prime numbers appear. Prime numbers, such as 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11, are divisible only by themselves and 1. Although they appear randomly as numbers get larger, mathematicians believe there is an underlying pattern governing their distribution. Riemann's hypothesis attempts to explain that pattern through a mathematical function called the Riemann zeta function.

In simple terms, it predicts that a particular set of solutions, known as the non-trivial zeros of this function, all fall on one specific line in a mathematical plane. Proving this would help mathematicians understand much more precisely how prime numbers are distributed.

The problem is among seven major mathematical challenges identified by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000. Each carries a $1 million prize for a valid solution. However, a proposed proof must first be published in a qualifying peer-reviewed journal, undergo at least two years of scrutiny and gain broad acceptance among mathematicians before the prize can be awarded.

The Riemann hypothesis remains officially unsolved. Moneycontrol News first published: Nov 21, 2026 11:51 am Discover the latest Business News , Sensex , and Nifty updates. extraction.body: It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics. “The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems. The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory. Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip . Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this … But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯. It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified. Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully. Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding. Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue. Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer. Meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.” Without being expressed in Lean, it is too early to say whether the proof checks out, much less if anyone understands it. In a brief introduction to his proof, which he said is the result of 12 years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.” This story has been updated to include that Alpöge’s Lean proof has been checked by independent sources.
