extraction.body: For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry . The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga. The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content. Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.” Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience. Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content. The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue. This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last. In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.” Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.” But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing? Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female . Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night , getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views. Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “ LICENSE YOUR FACE ” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content. A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.” Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A recent report in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.” How much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The company isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely. A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the company didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person said, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.” For other actors, however, the deals may be quite different. Plus, many creatives are understandably unsettled by signs of automation creeping into their industry. Until recently, microdramas seemed like a safe, entry-level gateway into the entertainment industry, where young actors could gain experience on sets and hone their craft. Now, companies are downsizing and producing content that doesn’t even require real actors. Jennifer Cooper, a longtime fan of the industry and founder of the consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, notes that there’s a lot of distrust of AI — both from audiences and within the microdrama industry itself. “Everyone’s been impacted by AI,” she said. “A lot of us have either lost work to AI or can see that it’s devastated this industry — [taking microdramas] from something that was a rare thing in the world, that was in growth, and providing work, particularly for young people…[and now] you know, it’s been decimated.” Questions of consent with AI likenesses have also dogged the industry (some creators claim they have had their likenesses stolen ), which is something that Shortical is obviously trying to address with its new face-licensing endeavor. Yet these licensing deals could also help to gig-ify the industry, creating a scenario in which creators pay a distributor for the chance to platform their content (or their face), then receive payouts based on the audience engagement they’re allowed to generate. Shortical recently partnered with a company called Payouts.com, which describes itself as a “payout infrastructure platform powering creator and gig economy disbursements at scale.” The plan is to create a system by which creatives can seamlessly interact with Shortical’s platform and get paid. Cooper believes the push towards AI in the industry is driven by broader financial trends. Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.” Despite all the investment in this space, Cooper seems skeptical that there is actually a huge audience for this kind of content. “Some of it does get views. passages: It’s a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list.
Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list.

Director Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel to his critically acclaimed Godzilla Minus One (2023) is everything one could want in a Godzilla movie: human pathos, great special effects, and, ultimately, two giant kaiju duking it out over who gets to destroy Japan (and eventually the world) the most.

Godzilla Minus On e was a massive hit, both in Japan—where it remains one of the highest grossing Japanese films ever—and worldwide, racking up $116 million globally and winning an Oscar for best visual effects.
Yamazaki said in interviews at the time that there had as yet been no talk of a sequel—while also hinting at future directions a sequel might explore.

Ghidorah, for instance, responds to a bombing attack by mutating into its famous three-headed King Ghidorah form, complete with a spiffy new superpower: a “gravity beam” that lets the creature levitate entire houses (and, at one point, Godzilla) into the sky before dropping them back to the ground.
And the kaiju vs. kaiju battle is spectacular in both scope and execution.
The family is just trying to live in peace after the devastation Godzilla inflicted on their country.
Alas, a new kaiju emerges, arriving via meteorite and using its tentacles to feed on local wildlife before morphing into a dragon-like creature that causes fresh rampaging destruction.
Fans of the genre will recognize this creature as Ghidorah , whose appearance in the film was teased in the various trailers.
Spoilers for Minus Zero but no major reveals until after the gallery.

As I wrote previously , Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One , setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption.

Yamazaki even managed to squeeze in what he called his “bucket-list” special effects shot inspired by a scene in 2008’s Cloverfield : Godzilla looming out of the Atlantic Ocean in front of the Statue of Liberty to wreck havoc on the statue and New York City in general.
And we saw a chunk of Godzilla’s remains start to regenerate, leaving things open for a sequel.

passages: Director Takashi Yamazaki ups the ante by pitting Godzilla against one of the monster’s greatest foes

It’s a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list. Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list. Director Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel to his critically acclaimed Godzilla Minus One (2023) is everything one could want in a Godzilla movie: human pathos, great special effects, and, ultimately, two giant kaiju duking it out over who gets to destroy Japan (and eventually the world) the most.
(Spoilers for the first film below. Spoilers for Minus Zero but no major reveals until after the gallery. We’ll give you a heads-up when we get there.)

As I wrote previously , Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One , setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption. That first film focused on kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who struggled with survivor’s guilt after he failed to take action when Godzilla attacked the Japanese base on Odo Island in 1945.

Knocked unconscious, Kōichi survived and awoke to find his parents and many others were killed in the World War II bombing of Tokyo. Kōichi rebuilt a life with a woman named Noriko (Minami Hamabe) and the orphaned baby she rescued, Akiko (Sae Nagatani). But then Godzilla re-emerged, and Kōichi resolved to die fighting the monster to atone for Odo Island. Kōichi saved the day and lived to tell the tale. He reunited with Noriko, who had a strange black bruise on her neck. And we saw a chunk of Godzilla’s remains start to regenerate, leaving things open for a sequel.

Godzilla Minus On e was a massive hit, both in Japan—where it remains one of the highest grossing Japanese films ever—and worldwide, racking up $116 million globally and winning an Oscar for best visual effects. Yamazaki said in interviews at the time that there had as yet been no talk of a sequel—while also hinting at future directions a sequel might explore. He later admitted it was way of planting a seed for what would become Godzilla Minus Zero .

Godzilla Minus Zero is set two years after the events of the first film, with Kamiki and Hamabe reprising their roles as Kōichi and Noriko, along with Nagatani as Akiko. The family is just trying to live in peace after the devastation Godzilla inflicted on their country. Alas, a new kaiju emerges, arriving via meteorite and using its tentacles to feed on local wildlife before morphing into a dragon-like creature that causes fresh rampaging destruction. Fans of the genre will recognize this creature as Ghidorah , whose appearance in the film was teased in the various trailers.

It isn’t long before Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka)—i.e., the dude with the magnificent wavy gray hair who is director of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau—seeks out Kōichi for help in dealing with this new kaiju threat. His team is able to track Ghidorah’s movements via electrical storms and other pertinent weather patterns, thanks to meteorologist Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa). But the team has no idea how they might defeat this new threat to life and infrastructure. It’s hardly a spoiler to note that at some point, a regenerated Godzilla will come into play.
(WARNING: significant spoilers appear below. Stop reading now if you haven’t seen the film.)

Yamazaki has retained the visual tone that made the film’s predecessor so striking; it feels like classic Godzilla fare of yore, just with 21st century cutting-edge visual effects. If anything, he’s upped his game on the special effects front, reflecting the larger production budget he had to work with. (It’s also the first Japanese movie filmed specifically for IMAX and it’s well-worth seeing in that format.)

Much of that budget went toward bringing the central monsters to cinematic life, and Godzilla Minus Zero does not disappoint. Ghidorah, for instance, responds to a bombing attack by mutating into its famous three-headed King Ghidorah form, complete with a spiffy new superpower: a “gravity beam” that lets the creature levitate entire houses (and, at one point, Godzilla) into the sky before dropping them back to the ground. And the kaiju vs. kaiju battle is spectacular in both scope and execution.

Yamazaki even managed to squeeze in what he called his “bucket-list” special effects shot inspired by a scene in 2008’s Cloverfield : Godzilla looming out of the Atlantic Ocean in front of the Statue of Liberty to wreck havoc on the statue and New York City in general. Granted, it occurs in a dream sequence of biologist Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka), who survived the Hiroshima blast that killed his wife and children and longs for revenge. And it’s not just indulgence on the director’s part: the scene reinforces the traditional theme of linking Godzilla to nuclear radiation and the horrors of the atomic bomb.

Nor does Yamazaki ignore the human factor via the dilemma of his nuclear family trio. Kōichi must wrestle with his conscience: how can he risk his life again to battle a kaiju when it could mean leaving Akiko an orphan yet again should he fail? Noriko is infected with Godzilla’s radioactive G-cells—the only human to survive the mutations in her own body for so long. But her time could be running out, plus they’ve kept her infection secret for fear she will be taken away by the government for experimentation. Sometimes doing the right thing comes at great personal cost, and watching these quite ordinary people grapple with that reality brings emotional depth to the film.
Godzilla Minus Zero is still playing in theaters.

extraction.body: The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee. Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies," according to the documents. From December through May, companies had made 3.4 million requests for sales of U.S. AI chips to China, the committee reported, citing those made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices . "Over the past month, the administration's handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk. The Bureau of Industry and Security has failed to enforce the rules, and Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration's policies," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said at a meeting of the panel Thursday at which members voted to release the documents. Spokespersons for Nvidia and AMD said their companies comply with U.S. export control laws. Nvidia argued it was following the Commerce Department regulations that were in effect at the time. A spokesperson from the Bureau of Industry and Security said it shared information with Congress on both approvals and denials of licenses for Nvidia's H200 and comparable chips. "Licensing decisions are the product of deliberation and consultation among multiple U.S. Government agencies," the spokesperson said. "The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China," Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told CNBC. On Tuesday, Nvidia reported $2.4 billion in quarterly revenue from H200 and related chip sales in China. In total, customers based in China and Hong Kong made up about 9.5% of all revenue. "AMD complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations," AMD said through a spokesperson. The approval of 879,000 AI chips is "not that many," Bernstein Senior Analyst Stacy Rasgon told CNBC, adding that this news is not surprising. "It doesn't sound to me like they're approving everything they got willy nilly," Rasgon said of the Commerce Department. With 879,000 approvals out of 3.4 million requested AI chip sales, he added, "There was a process in place, and it sounds like they approved about one out of every four." Despite a rapid succession of China export controls on AI chips that started under the Biden administration in 2022, Nvidia and AMD both re-engineered some chips to comply and be sold legally in China. And in December, Trump said Nvidia could ship H200s, its older generation Hopper chips, to "approved customers in China" if the U.S. got a 25% cut of sales. The U.S. then licensed Nvidia H200 sales to Alibaba , Tencent, ByteDance and other Chinese companies, although sales were limited because Beijing didn't approve large-scale imports, chip analyst Patrick Moorhead of Moor Insights & Strategy told CNBC last week. H200 sales numbers remained low due to those restrictions on China's end. Nvidia said H200 shipments to China made up less than 1% of data center revenue for the quarter that ended in July. "In the grand context of the size of this market and how much they're shipping, it's a rounding error. It's tiny," Rasgon told CNBC. The committee cited the Export Control Reform Act as justification for releasing the data. The panel said the law allows it to declassify and release export data if it "determines that the withholding of the following information is contrary to the national interest." The license requests released by the Foreign Affairs Committee include requests to sell to major firms including ByteDance, Tesla (Shanghai) and Baidu . The release of documents comes in the wake of Jensen Huang 's resignation from the chip supplier Nvidia after news surfaced that he had several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that led to concerns about Nvidia chips being diverted to China. In the weeks since, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have called for legislation to be passed that would impose stricter export controls on the sale of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries. "The license information we are disclosing today will help inform the American public about how BIS has handled licenses for Nvidia H200 and equivalent AMD chips to China. The public has the right to know how these decisions were made," Meeks said. Mast said two of the firms listed in Nvidia license applications to BIS — Maginfra and New Matrix — are suspected "smuggling fronts." The New York Times reported in November that both companies had empty offices and had ties to companies under national security sanctions. "Both are fake companies. If BIS approved the sale of these chips to these firms, obviously that is of tremendous concern to us — especially given that President Trump made clear last year that the sale of any AI chips to China will have very real national security conditions," Mast said at the Thursday meeting. Maginfra and New Matrix did not reply to requests for comment. Shares of AMD fell Thursday after the investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging the company "has its own China problem." The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers." CNBC did not independently verify this information. Fallout from the Huang scandal on Capitol Hill has intensified in the last week, as lawmakers question the degree to which the former head of Nvidia's relationship with the suspected Chinese spy could have jeopardized national security and American AI dominance. Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels Dec. 2. Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., announced on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had also agreed to testify. Lutnick has come under fire over his relationship to Huang and for his failure to take action on Megaspeed , the Singaporean company where Alice Huang , with whom the former Nvidia CEO had an affair, was an executive until 2025. U.S. investigators suspect Megaspeed diverted Nvidia chips to China. Amid that criticism, the Commerce Department on Monday issued an interim final rule to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia's advancing computing power from data centers in third countries. The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release.

The requested buyers included Alibaba , Tencent, Baidu and BYD, and some of the companies were believed by the Pentagon to have links to the People's Liberation Army, the FT reported [3] . The committee had said on Thursday, Nov. 19, that the Commerce Department approved sales of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies, out of 3.4 million that Nvidia and AMD asked to sell [1] [2] . Committee Chairman Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, used his authority under the Export Control Reform Act to publish the export license application information for China, the committee said [1] . It called the release "the most detailed public disclosure in the history of the Export Control Reform Act." CNBC reported that members voted at a committee meeting to release the documents and that the approval figure is as of May 2026 [2] . The Bureau of Industry and Security approved the "export, re-export or transfer" of 879,868 chips, the FT reported [3] . The paper did not name the chip models in the copy we reviewed. The Register, which also reviewed the disclosure, reported that BIS refused Nvidia applications to sell 610,000 chips to Alibaba and 508,000 to ByteDance, the owner of TikTok [4] . It quoted Mast as saying that "every Nvidia and AMD application stated that the proposed transfer posed a 'low' risk of diversion" [4] . AMD said it "complied with applicable US export control laws and regulations" and maintained "rigorous compliance procedures" across its global operations, the FT reported; Nvidia did not immediately respond [3] . AMD shares fell 7.7% on Thursday after two reports linked to the short seller Hunterbrook raised questions about its ties to Beijing, according to the same report [3] . Semafor reported that the disclosure has widened scrutiny in Washington of the semiconductor industry as a whole, not only Nvidia, and cited Caixin as reporting that China's tech giants are "reeling" from the prospect of new US restrictions [5] . The FT also reported that California's attorney general subpoenaed Nvidia on Thursday, seeking information on whether its advanced chips or confidential information reached China and whether it misled investors [3] . The committee said the approvals by the Bureau of Industry and Security, the Commerce agency that licenses exports, included chips for companies the Department of War has designated as Chinese Military Companies, "like Alibaba and Tencent" [1] . CNBC also named Alibaba and Tencent among the buyers [2] . The committee's release does not break the total down by chip model. Rep. Gregory Meeks, the committee's top Democrat, referred to Nvidia's H200 "and equivalent AMD chips" in his comments, according to CNBC [2] . The committee said the documents include requests by Nvidia "to depend on possible chip-smuggling fronts" for sales to Chinese companies [1] . Mast named two firms listed in Nvidia's applications, Maginfra and New Matrix, as suspected "smuggling fronts," called them "fake companies," and said BIS approving sales to them would be of "tremendous concern," CNBC reported [2] . The New York Times reported this month that both had empty offices and ties to sanctioned companies; CNBC said it had not independently verified that [2] . Meeks said the administration's handling of chip export controls "has put our national security and technology edge at risk" and that BIS "has failed to enforce the rules," according to CNBC [2] . Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott said this week that Huang had agreed to testify . The disclosure lands in a week of tighter China chip policy. On Monday, Commerce issued an interim final rule closing a loophole that let Chinese companies lease Nvidia computing power from data centers in third countries, CNBC reported [2] . TSMC and Samsung curbed some shipments to Chinese customers as a new US rule took effect, and Alibaba said it is training its next Qwen model on its own chips . Commerce approved, but had not shipped, 75,000 chips for Alibaba, 43,000 for Baidu, 4,000 for BYD and 150,000 for Tencent.

“AMD complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,” an AMD spokesperson told the DCNF. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity.”
Applicants asked Commerce to approve exports of 3,444,160 chips for “PRC [People’s Republic of China] companies” through May 11, the records show.

The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said the export license records prove the department is transparent and was following a Jan. 15 licensing review rule , but the agency announced a new rule Monday, “Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors,” to crack down on chip exports.

“Yesterday’s disclosure shows that the Department of Commerce has a long track record of transparency with Congress about licensing activity for the H200 and equivalent chips, including both approvals and rejections,” a BIS spokesperson said in a statement to the DCNF.

extraction.body: The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee. Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies," according to the documents. From December through May, companies had made 3.4 million requests for sales of U.S. AI chips to China, the committee reported, citing those made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices . "Over the past month, the administration's handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk. The Bureau of Industry and Security has failed to enforce the rules, and Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration's policies," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said at a meeting of the panel Thursday at which members voted to release the documents. Spokespersons for Nvidia and AMD said their companies comply with U.S. export control laws. Nvidia argued it was following the Commerce Department regulations that were in effect at the time. A spokesperson from the Bureau of Industry and Security said it shared information with Congress on both approvals and denials of licenses for Nvidia's H200 and comparable chips. "Licensing decisions are the product of deliberation and consultation among multiple U.S. Government agencies," the spokesperson said. "The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China," Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told CNBC. On Tuesday, Nvidia reported $2.4 billion in quarterly revenue from H200 and related chip sales in China. In total, customers based in China and Hong Kong made up about 9.5% of all revenue. "AMD complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations," AMD said through a spokesperson. The approval of 879,000 AI chips is "not that many," Bernstein Senior Analyst Stacy Rasgon told CNBC, adding that this news is not surprising. "It doesn't sound to me like they're approving everything they got willy nilly," Rasgon said of the Commerce Department. With 879,000 approvals out of 3.4 million requested AI chip sales, he added, "There was a process in place, and it sounds like they approved about one out of every four." Despite a rapid succession of China export controls on AI chips that started under the Biden administration in 2022, Nvidia and AMD both re-engineered some chips to comply and be sold legally in China. And in December, Trump said Nvidia could ship H200s, its older generation Hopper chips, to "approved customers in China" if the U.S. got a 25% cut of sales. The U.S. then licensed Nvidia H200 sales to Alibaba , Tencent, ByteDance and other Chinese companies, although sales were limited because Beijing didn't approve large-scale imports, chip analyst Patrick Moorhead of Moor Insights & Strategy told CNBC last week. H200 sales numbers remained low due to those restrictions on China's end. Nvidia said H200 shipments to China made up less than 1% of data center revenue for the quarter that ended in July. "In the grand context of the size of this market and how much they're shipping, it's a rounding error. It's tiny," Rasgon told CNBC. The committee cited the Export Control Reform Act as justification for releasing the data. The panel said the law allows it to declassify and release export data if it "determines that the withholding of the following information is contrary to the national interest." The license requests released by the Foreign Affairs Committee include requests to sell to major firms including ByteDance, Tesla (Shanghai) and Baidu . The release of documents comes in the wake of Jensen Huang 's resignation from the chip supplier Nvidia after news surfaced that he had several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that led to concerns about Nvidia chips being diverted to China. In the weeks since, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have called for legislation to be passed that would impose stricter export controls on the sale of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries. "The license information we are disclosing today will help inform the American public about how BIS has handled licenses for Nvidia H200 and equivalent AMD chips to China. The public has the right to know how these decisions were made," Meeks said. Mast said two of the firms listed in Nvidia license applications to BIS — Maginfra and New Matrix — are suspected "smuggling fronts." The New York Times reported in November that both companies had empty offices and had ties to companies under national security sanctions. "Both are fake companies. If BIS approved the sale of these chips to these firms, obviously that is of tremendous concern to us — especially given that President Trump made clear last year that the sale of any AI chips to China will have very real national security conditions," Mast said at the Thursday meeting. Maginfra and New Matrix did not reply to requests for comment. Shares of AMD fell Thursday after the investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging the company "has its own China problem." The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers." CNBC did not independently verify this information. Fallout from the Huang scandal on Capitol Hill has intensified in the last week, as lawmakers question the degree to which the former head of Nvidia's relationship with the suspected Chinese spy could have jeopardized national security and American AI dominance. Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels Dec. 2. Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., announced on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had also agreed to testify. Lutnick has come under fire over his relationship to Huang and for his failure to take action on Megaspeed , the Singaporean company where Alice Huang , with whom the former Nvidia CEO had an affair, was an executive until 2025. U.S. investigators suspect Megaspeed diverted Nvidia chips to China. Amid that criticism, the Commerce Department on Monday issued an interim final rule to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia's advancing computing power from data centers in third countries. The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release.

Kathy Hochul broke ground November 19, 2026, at the University at Buffalo on a supercomputing center that will house Empire AI Gamma, the consortium’s third phase. The project is intended to give researchers across New York’s universities access to more computing power. The Empire AI Research Computing Center will occupy 46,000 square feet on Service Center Road on UB’s North Campus. Hochul’s office says the permanent facility is expected to be completed by early 2028. UB gives a later target for becoming operational: late summer 2028 . The governor’s office describes Empire AI as a public-private initiative worth more than $500 million . That figure covers the initiative, not just this building. Its organizing principle is shared access: bringing public and private research institutions together around computing resources that, the state says, no single university could afford independently. Empire AI’s earlier systems have been operating at UB’s Downtown Campus. Empire AI Board Chair Tom Secunda said the initiative now has more than 1,500 registered users and hundreds of research projects underway. Alpha launched in 2024 with a philanthropic contribution from the Simons Foundation. Beta, a $40 million supercomputer at UB, became fully operational in August 2026. According to UB, the NVIDIA-powered Beta system delivers 11 times Alpha’s AI training capacity, 40 times its inference performance and eight times its data storage. For the permanent center, SUNY Chancellor John B. King Jr. described the goal as working with larger datasets, larger models and more complex simulations, with the hope of making discoveries faster. UB plans to capture heat generated by the computing center and use it to warm buildings across the North Campus. The university presents that reuse as part of its effort to decarbonize the campus. UB says a dry cooler will remove heat using outside air, reducing reliance on water-intensive cooling methods. Buffalo’s cooler climate is expected to help conserve energy and water, with a high-efficiency water-cooling system needed only during the region’s hottest months. Research continues while the permanent home is built. UB says its existing Empire AI projects include early-childhood education, drug discovery, wildfire prediction and quantum materials—work already using the shared infrastructure before Gamma arrives. extraction.body: BUFFALO, N.Y. (WBNG) — On Thursday, Nov. 19, Gov. Kathy Hochul broke ground on a permanent home for EmpireAI at the University at Buffalo, beginning the next phase of development for the state’s artificial intelligence research initiative. The planned facility, known as EmpireAI Gamma, is intended to expand computing resources available to researchers at participating public and private universities across the state. “The technology of AI is very complicated, but our mission is simple; we’re not distracted,” Hochul said. “We know what we must do here in New York and to make AI work for the benefit of all New Yorkers and ultimately all Americans as they follow our lead.” EmpireAI was first announced in Hochul’s 2024 State of the State address and is now a public-private initiative worth more than $500 million, according to Hochul’s office. “The decisions we make today in laboratories and boardrooms and universities like this one, those decisions and the ramifications will echo for generations to come, across our economy and our families and the very fabric of how we live,” Hochul said. The administration says the computing resources are already supporting research in medicine, climate science and advanced manufacturing. Hochul highlighted research at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute on lung cancer diagnosis, work at Cornell University on prostate cancer treatments and a Columbia University project to improve weather tracking. “I wanted to give our academic researchers the most powerful technology that any single university could offer; there is nothing that competes with this,” Hochul said. “This is more powerful than anything that’s in public hands for sure, but rivals what private companies have in their own.” The governor also called for safeguards in AI development and said students should learn how to use the technology. “So, no matter what they do here in New York, we’re demanding that AI be developed with appropriate safeguards and make sure that this incredible tool is never used as a deadly weapon,” Hochul said.

coreStoryFacts.text: New York’s shared AI research infrastructure is getting a permanent home .
Kathy Hochul broke ground November 19, 2026, at the University at Buffalo on a supercomputing center that will house Empire AI Gamma, the consortium’s third phase.
The investment expands shared compute access for university researchers, but the stated funding figure applies to the broader initiative, not the building alone.
The Empire AI Research Computing Center will occupy 46,000 square feet on Service Center Road on UB’s North Campus.
The governor’s office describes Empire AI as a public-private initiative worth more than $500 million .
Its organizing principle is shared access: bringing public and private research institutions together around computing resources that, the state says, no single university could afford independently.
For the permanent center, SUNY Chancellor John B.
Research continues while the permanent home is built.
Hochul’s office says the permanent facility is expected to be completed by early 2028.
Kathy Hochul broke ground on a permanent home for EmpireAI at the University at Buffalo, beginning the next phase of development for the state’s artificial intelligence research initiative.
“The technology of AI is very complicated, but our mission is simple; we’re not distracted,” Hochul said.
“We know what we must do here in New York and to make AI work for the benefit of all New Yorkers and ultimately all Americans as they follow our lead.”
EmpireAI was first announced in Hochul’s 2024 State of the State address and is now a public-private initiative worth more than $500 million, according to Hochul’s office.

Kathy Hochul broke ground November 19, 2026, at the University at Buffalo on a supercomputing center that will house Empire AI Gamma, the consortium’s third phase. The project is intended to give researchers across New York’s universities access to more computing power. The Empire AI Research Computing Center will occupy 46,000 square feet on Service Center Road on UB’s North Campus. Hochul’s office says the permanent facility is expected to be completed by early 2028. UB gives a later target for becoming operational: late summer 2028 . The governor’s office describes Empire AI as a public-private initiative worth more than $500 million . That figure covers the initiative, not just this building. Its organizing principle is shared access: bringing public and private research institutions together around computing resources that, the state says, no single university could afford independently. Empire AI’s earlier systems have been operating at UB’s Downtown Campus. Empire AI Board Chair Tom Secunda said the initiative now has more than 1,500 registered users and hundreds of research projects underway. Alpha launched in 2024 with a philanthropic contribution from the Simons Foundation. Beta, a $40 million supercomputer at UB, became fully operational in August 2026. According to UB, the NVIDIA-powered Beta system delivers 11 times Alpha’s AI training capacity, 40 times its inference performance and eight times its data storage. For the permanent center, SUNY Chancellor John B. King Jr. described the goal as working with larger datasets, larger models and more complex simulations, with the hope of making discoveries faster. UB plans to capture heat generated by the computing center and use it to warm buildings across the North Campus. The university presents that reuse as part of its effort to decarbonize the campus. UB says a dry cooler will remove heat using outside air, reducing reliance on water-intensive cooling methods. Buffalo’s cooler climate is expected to help conserve energy and water, with a high-efficiency water-cooling system needed only during the region’s hottest months. Research continues while the permanent home is built. UB says its existing Empire AI projects include early-childhood education, drug discovery, wildfire prediction and quantum materials—work already using the shared infrastructure before Gamma arrives. The governor’s office describes Empire AI as a public-private initiative worth more than $500 million . That figure covers the initiative, not just this building. Its organizing principle is shared access: bringing public and private research institutions together around computing resources that, the state says, no single university could afford independently.

Empire AI’s earlier systems have been operating at UB’s Downtown Campus. Empire AI Board Chair Tom Secunda said the initiative now has more than 1,500 registered users and hundreds of research projects underway.
Alpha launched in 2024 with a philanthropic contribution from the Simons Foundation. Beta, a $40 million supercomputer at UB, became fully operational in August 2026.
According to UB, the NVIDIA-powered Beta system delivers 11 times Alpha’s AI training capacity, 40 times its inference performance and eight times its data storage.
For the permanent center, SUNY Chancellor John B. King Jr. described the goal as working with larger datasets, larger models and more complex simulations, with the hope of making discoveries faster.
UB plans to capture heat generated by the computing center and use it to warm buildings across the North Campus. The university presents that reuse as part of its effort to decarbonize the campus.

UB says a dry cooler will remove heat using outside air, reducing reliance on water-intensive cooling methods. Buffalo’s cooler climate is expected to help conserve energy and water, with a high-efficiency water-cooling system needed only during the region’s hottest months.

Research continues while the permanent home is built. UB says its existing Empire AI projects include early-childhood education, drug discovery, wildfire prediction and quantum materials—work already using the shared infrastructure before Gamma arrives.

extraction.body: BUFFALO, N.Y. (WBNG) — On Thursday, Nov. 19, Gov. Kathy Hochul broke ground on a permanent home for EmpireAI at the University at Buffalo, beginning the next phase of development for the state’s artificial intelligence research initiative. The planned facility, known as EmpireAI Gamma, is intended to expand computing resources available to researchers at participating public and private universities across the state. “The technology of AI is very complicated, but our mission is simple; we’re not distracted,” Hochul said. “We know what we must do here in New York and to make AI work for the benefit of all New Yorkers and ultimately all Americans as they follow our lead.” EmpireAI was first announced in Hochul’s 2024 State of the State address and is now a public-private initiative worth more than $500 million, according to Hochul’s office. “The decisions we make today in laboratories and boardrooms and universities like this one, those decisions and the ramifications will echo for generations to come, across our economy and our families and the very fabric of how we live,” Hochul said. The administration says the computing resources are already supporting research in medicine, climate science and advanced manufacturing. Hochul highlighted research at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute on lung cancer diagnosis, work at Cornell University on prostate cancer treatments and a Columbia University project to improve weather tracking. “I wanted to give our academic researchers the most powerful technology that any single university could offer; there is nothing that competes with this,” Hochul said. “This is more powerful than anything that’s in public hands for sure, but rivals what private companies have in their own.” The governor also called for safeguards in AI development and said students should learn how to use the technology. “So, no matter what they do here in New York, we’re demanding that AI be developed with appropriate safeguards and make sure that this incredible tool is never used as a deadly weapon,” Hochul said.
